Beyond Monotonicity: Stochastic Online Optimization
under Semi-Bandit Feedback

Tsubasa Harada Affiliation: Institute of Science Tokyo    Yasushi Kawase Affiliation: Chuo University    Hanna Sumita Affiliation: Institute of Science Tokyo
Abstract

We study stochastic online optimization (SOO) under semi-bandit feedback, in which a policy adaptively observes nn independent random variables with unknown distributions in each of TT rounds, and only the observed values are available for learning. Monotonicity with respect to first-order stochastic dominance enables general reductions for learning SOO, but it fails in natural problems where observations change future feasibility, resource use, or reference points. We provide an algorithm that runs the dynamic program for the optimal policy with each expectation replaced by its most optimistic value over a confidence set of distributions. Its regret is governed by the level-set complexity sis_{i} of the values computed by this dynamic program as functions of the iith variable, that is, the number of intervals needed to describe their superlevel sets. For rewards in [0,1][0,1], the regret is O~​(S​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST}) without this monotonicity, where S=∑i=1nmin⁡{si,ki}S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{s_{i},k_{i}\} and kik_{i} is the support size of the iith distribution, which may be infinite when sis_{i} is finite. In particular, when the level-set complexities are bounded by a constant, the regret is O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}), even for continuous distributions. The algorithm requires no knowledge of sis_{i}, kik_{i}, or the supports, and it also achieves regret O~​(n​k​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nkT}) for supports of size at most kk without any level-set condition, which improves the previous bound O~​(n​(k​T+k))\widetilde{O}(n(\sqrt{kT}+k)) for FSD-monotone problems. We also prove a lower bound of Ω⁡(min⁡{T,S​T})\Omega(\min\{T,\sqrt{ST}\}) for all positive integers s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n} with ki=2​si+1k_{i}=2s_{i}+1, which holds even under full feedback and matches the upper bound up to logarithmic factors. As applications, we obtain regret O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}) for the following problems, none of which is monotone under stochastic dominance: stochastic Boolean function evaluation, the full-information secretary problem, optimal stopping with loss aversion, scheduling with deadlines and correlated stochastic knapsack with unimodal rewards, and overbooking with group reservations.

Keywords: stochastic online optimization, semi-bandit feedback, regret, level sets

1 Introduction

Stochastic online optimization (SOO) is a framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. The input consists of nn independent random variables, and a policy adaptively chooses the next action based on the values observed so far. This framework includes optimal stopping problems such as Pandora’s box [37] and prophet inequalities [34, 25], as well as stochastic probing [20], stochastic submodular optimization [2], and other stochastic combinatorial optimization problems.

Ghuge, Zhuo, Agarwal, and Nagarajan [15] (a preliminary version appeared at FOCS 2024) introduced a general framework for learning SOO when the distributions are unknown, in which the same instance is played for TT rounds. In each round, the learner chooses a policy and receives semi-bandit feedback, which consists of the values of the variables observed during the execution of the policy. The goal is to minimize the regret, which is the cumulative loss in expected reward compared with the optimal policy that knows the distributions. Their framework assumes monotonicity with respect to first-order stochastic dominance (FSD), called FSD monotonicity, which means that replacing each distribution by a stochastically dominating one never decreases (or never increases) the optimal expected reward. Under this assumption, running an algorithm for known distributions on optimistic distributions that dominate the true ones (or are dominated by them in the latter case) achieves regret O~​(n​(k​T+k))\widetilde{O}(n(\sqrt{kT}+k)) for rewards in [0,1][0,1] and supports of size at most kk [15], where O~\widetilde{O} suppresses logarithmic factors. They also extend their framework to continuous distributions under additional assumptions on the threshold structure of policies and the regularity of the reward functions.

These results leave the following question. Can the regret grow as T\sqrt{T} without FSD monotonicity, with a polynomial dependence on nn that does not involve the number of policies or observation histories, even for continuous distributions? Treating each deterministic policy as an arm already yields T\sqrt{T} dependence when there are finitely many policies, but the regret then grows with their number. We answer this question affirmatively, and our results extend the framework of Ghuge, Zhuo, Agarwal, and Nagarajan beyond FSD monotonicity and improve their regret bound.

FSD monotonicity fails in natural problems, and Section 4 studies five of them. In stochastic Boolean function evaluation (SBFE) [12], binary variables are tested at a cost until a known Boolean function is determined, and the expected cost of evaluating the majority function is largest when successes and failures are balanced. In the full-information secretary problem [16, 13], a stochastically larger later value makes accepting an earlier candidate less likely to succeed but waiting more likely to succeed. In optimal stopping with loss aversion [24], a large early value raises the reference point and lowers the utility of later candidates. In scheduling with deadlines [11] and its special case, correlated stochastic knapsack [19], a larger processing time or size can increase the reward of the current job or item but leaves less room for the others. In overbooking with group reservations [35], more arrivals reduce refunds but increase the cost of exceeding capacity.

Under FSD monotonicity, optimistic distributions can be constructed by shifting probability mass in the empirical distributions upward or downward according to the direction of monotonicity. Without this property, the optimistic distribution can depend on the observation history and need not be confined to a single direction. The dependence on history already appears in SBFE for the majority of three variables (Figure 1): optimism favors increasing the success probability of the next test after observing 11, but decreasing it after observing 00, since agreement determines the majority. The DP for an optimal policy makes this dependence explicit through expectations of optimal continuation values, the maximum expected rewards obtainable from each decision point given the observations so far. Replacing each expectation by its supremum over the corresponding confidence set yields optimistic continuation values by backward induction, provided the confidence sets contain the true distributions.

The main challenge is to control the estimation errors in the expectations of these data-dependent values uniformly over all observation histories, with no dependence on the number of histories. Uniform control over all bounded functions introduces a dependence on the support size and can be vacuous for continuous distributions, so the analysis must exploit the structure of these values. Moreover, summing variance-insensitive bounds on the local expectation errors yields a regret bound linear in nn, even when the continuation values are monotone in the newly observed variable. We address these issues through the level-set structure of the optimistic continuation values and a variance-sensitive analysis of the accumulated expectation errors.

1.1 Our Contributions

We refer to the iith random variable as coordinate ii. For a function of one observed coordinate, its level-set complexity is the smallest integer ss such that every superlevel set is the intersection of the coordinate’s domain with a union of at most ss intervals. Our algorithm replaces each expectation in the DP by its supremum over a confidence set of distributions, i.e., optimistic continuation values. Our main assumption, which we call the level-set condition, bounds by sis_{i} the level-set complexity of the optimistic continuation values after coordinate ii is revealed, for any possible confidence sets (Assumption 3.1).

Regret Upper Bound. With rewards in [0,1][0,1], let kik_{i} be the number of support points of the distribution DiD_{i} of coordinate ii, which may be infinite, and let S=∑i=1nmin⁡{si,ki}S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{s_{i},k_{i}\}. The algorithm’s regret satisfies RT=O~​(S​T)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST}) against the optimal policy (Theorem 3.2). This guarantee does not require FSD monotonicity or finite supports, and the algorithm requires no knowledge of sis_{i} or kik_{i}.

In particular, when the level-set complexities are bounded by a constant, the regret is O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}), even for continuous distributions and without FSD monotonicity. If each distribution has at most kk support points, the regret is O~​(n​k​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nkT}) even when the supports are unknown and without any condition on the level-set complexity (Corollary 3.3). In the setting of Ghuge, Zhuo, Agarwal, and Nagarajan, this improves their bound O~​(n​(k​T+k))\widetilde{O}(n(\sqrt{kT}+k)) without requiring FSD monotonicity. For FSD-monotone problems with finite domains, as in their framework, it also suffices to run an exact or α\alpha-approximation algorithm for known distributions once per round on a single product distribution chosen from the confidence sets (Proposition 3.4), with α\alpha-regret O~​(n​k​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nkT}) for supports of size at most kk. If the problem is realization-monotone, that is, all rewards and all sets of feasible actions are monotone in the observed values in a common direction, then si=1s_{i}=1 (Section 3.2), and the regret is O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}). This applies to the prophet inequality, Pandora’s box, and stochastic knapsack with fixed rewards after rescaling the rewards to [0,1][0,1], and for the first two with finite domains, each round runs in polynomial time by Proposition 3.4. The bound O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}) does not depend on the support sizes, whereas the finite-support bound in [15] grows with kk. Table 1 compares our general bounds with previous ones.

Regret Lower Bound. We complement our upper bounds with matching lower bounds, which show that their dependence on the level-set complexities and the support sizes is necessary. For any integers T,s1,…,sn≥1T,s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\geq 1, we construct a problem satisfying Assumption 3.1 with these sis_{i} such that, for every learning algorithm, some product distribution with 2​si+12s_{i}+1 support points for coordinate ii forces regret Ω⁡(min⁡{T,S​T})\Omega(\min\{T,\sqrt{ST}\}), even under full feedback (Theorem 3.6). Here, full feedback means that all nn coordinates are observed in each round. Hence, the worst-case regret over the problems with given s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n} is Θ~​(min⁡{T,S​T})\widetilde{\Theta}(\min\{T,\sqrt{ST}\}) with S=∑isiS=\sum_{i}s_{i}. Since coordinate ii of this instance has 2​si+12s_{i}+1 support points, the dependence on the support sizes in Corollary 3.3 cannot be improved in the worst case either. For realization-monotone problems, our bound O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}) is also tight up to logarithmic factors, since Ghuge, Zhuo, Agarwal, and Nagarajan [15] observed a lower bound of Ω⁡(n​T)\Omega(\sqrt{nT}) under semi-bandit feedback by a reduction from multi-armed bandits, and their instance with binary coordinates is realization-monotone.

Applications. For the five applications, we verify the level-set condition directly for SBFE, where si=1s_{i}=1 since the variables are binary, and for the full-information secretary problem and optimal stopping with loss aversion, where si=2s_{i}=2. Scheduling with deadlines, including correlated stochastic knapsack, and overbooking with group reservations require an extension, since a sum of functions with small level-set complexity need not have small complexity itself. Theorem 3.7 handles continuation values decomposed into an immediate reward collected when a coordinate is revealed and a residual reward collected later. It assumes that the immediate rewards have bounded level-set complexity, are nonnegative, and sum to at most 1 in each round, and that larger revealed values cannot increase the residual rewards or enlarge future sets of feasible actions. Together, the two theorems yield regret O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}) for all five applications after rescaling the rewards to [0,1][0,1], provided that, in scheduling, the reward functions have bounded level-set complexity and the observed processing time and reward identify the outcome. For the full-information secretary problem, the bound holds for every known distribution over arrival orders.

A refinement of Theorem 3.2 yields O~​(S​T​p​(1−p)+S)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST\,p(1-p)}+S), where pp is the optimal value (Proposition 3.5), and Proposition 3.8 provides an analogous refinement of Theorem 3.7. These refinements yield sharper regret bounds for all five applications in their original units.

Computation Time. For computation, we reduce each optimistic update to a linear program (LP) over the masses of the sample points and the intervals between them, which is the dual of a minimum-cost flow problem. Its coefficients are the suprema of the optimistic continuation value on these parts. Given these suprema, each round runs in time polynomial in nn, tt, and the size of the decision tree (Proposition A.3), which can be exponential in nn, and the suprema themselves can be hard to compute in general. Each supremum reduces to evaluations of the optimistic continuation value at finitely many points when the domains are finite, or when the domains are [0,1][0,1] and the values are continuous and either quasi-convex or monotone on each of finitely many known intervals. When the values are Lipschitz, approximate evaluations on a grid increase the regret by at most 1 and take time polynomial in nn, TT, and the Lipschitz constant. As in a DP for known distributions, these evaluations can be organized by states when the rewards and the sets of feasible actions depend on the observations only through a state, apart from rewards collected along the way, and each round then runs in time polynomial in nn, tt, the size of the tree, and the number of pairs of a node and a state reachable through the evaluation points (Proposition A.4). For overbooking with group reservations, this yields time polynomial in nn, tt, the number of allowed sets of accepted groups, and the total group size (Appendix A.3). Each round also runs in polynomial time for optimal stopping with loss aversion when each domain is [0,1][0,1] or finite (Appendix A.3) and for the full-information secretary problem with finite domains and a fixed arrival order (Section 4.2), and it runs in time O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) for SBFE with threshold functions (Section 4.1).

1.2 Technical Overview

Our algorithm follows the principle of optimism in the face of uncertainty. In our formulation (Section 2), the decision points are the nodes of a finite tree whose edges either reveal a coordinate or stop, and the observed values are carried along the path. For each coordinate, we construct from the samples collected so far a confidence set that contains the true distribution with high probability, and we replace each expectation in the DP by its supremum over this set. If the true distributions belong to the confidence sets, backward induction shows that the resulting values are at least the true optimal values. Each DP update takes the supremum separately, and different nodes and observations may use different distributions from the same confidence set.

The main technical step translates this local optimism into a global regret bound. The confidence sets impose Bernstein-type constraints on the probabilities of intervals. For two distributions P,QP,Q in the same confidence set built from m≥1m\geq 1 samples and a [0,1][0,1]-valued function ϕ\phi with level-set complexity at most ss, Lemma 5.4(b) yields

|𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]−𝔼X∼P​[ϕ⁡(X)]|≤O~​(s/m​VarX∼P⁡(ϕ⁡(X))+s/m).\left|\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[\phi(X)]\right|\leq\widetilde{O}\!\left(\sqrt{{s}/{m}}\,\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X))}+{s}/{m}\right).

We prove this bound by integrating the probability errors over the superlevel sets of ϕ\phi, each of which is a union of at most ss intervals. A variance-sensitive inequality for this integral yields the square-root dependence on VarX∼P⁡(ϕ⁡(X))\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X)) (Lemma 5.3).

Fix the history before round tt and suppose that the confidence sets contain the true distributions. Let Yt,hY_{t,h} be the optimistic continuation value at the node visited at stage hh, and let dt,h=Yt,h−𝔼⁡[Yt,h+1∣ℱt,h]d_{t,h}=Y_{t,h}-\mathbb{E}[Y_{t,h+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t,h}] and wt,h=Var⁡(Yt,h+1∣ℱt,h)w_{t,h}=\operatorname{Var}(Y_{t,h+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t,h}), where ℱt,h\mathcal{F}_{t,h} is the history through stage hh. Since 𝔼⁡[Yt,0]\mathbb{E}[Y_{t,0}] is at least the optimal value and the last Yt,hY_{t,h} is the reward, the expected regret in this round is at most 𝔼⁡[∑hdt,h]\mathbb{E}[\sum_{h}d_{t,h}]. Let Ni,tN_{i,t} be the number of rounds before round tt in which coordinate ii was revealed, and let Ii,tI_{i,t} indicate whether coordinate ii is revealed on an edge in round tt. Up to logarithmic factors, the proof combines three bounds:

dt,h≲si​wt,hNi,t+1+siNi,t+1,𝔼⁡[∑hwt,h]≤1,∑t=1TIi,tNi,t+1≤1+log⁡T.d_{t,h}\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{s_{i}w_{t,h}}{N_{i,t}+1}}+\frac{s_{i}}{N_{i,t}+1},\qquad\mathbb{E}\biggl[\sum_{h}w_{t,h}\biggr]\leq 1,\qquad\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{I_{i,t}}{N_{i,t}+1}\leq 1+\log T.

In the first bound, ii is the coordinate revealed at stage hh. The first bound follows from the expectation bound above, and it is the only place where level-set complexity is used. If DiD_{i} has ki<sik_{i}<s_{i} support points, a one-sided version of the expectation bound (Lemma 5.5) yields the first bound with kik_{i} in place of sis_{i}, and hence the regret depends on S=∑imin⁡{si,ki}S=\sum_{i}\min\{s_{i},k_{i}\}. The second bound holds because (Yt,h)h(Y_{t,h})_{h} is a supermartingale with values in [0,1][0,1], and telescoping the squares Yt,h2Y_{t,h}^{2} bounds the sum of the conditional variances. The third bound holds because Ni,tN_{i,t} increases by one in each round in which coordinate ii is revealed. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality then yields the leading term S​T\sqrt{ST}.

For the lower bound, we construct an instance with SS unknown signs θi​j\theta_{ij}, where j∈[si]j\in[s_{i}] for coordinate ii. Each coordinate ii equals a special value ⊥\bot with probability 1−si/(2​S)1-s_{i}/(2S). Otherwise, it takes a value (j,y)(j,y), where the index j∈[si]j\in[s_{i}] is uniform and the sign y∈{−1,+1}y\in\{-1,+1\} equals θi​j\theta_{ij} with probability (1+ε)/2(1+\varepsilon)/2. Before receiving observations in a round, the learner chooses a prediction y^i​j\widehat{y}_{ij} of the observed sign yy for each possible pair (i,j)(i,j). The reward is 1 if exactly one coordinate differs from ⊥\bot and its sign is predicted correctly, and 0 otherwise. Each prediction y^i​j\widehat{y}_{ij} that differs from θi​j\theta_{ij} reduces the expected reward by Θ⁡(ε/S)\Theta(\varepsilon/S) relative to predicting θi​j\theta_{ij}.

Two environments differing in one sign have one-sample Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence O⁡(ε2/S)O(\varepsilon^{2}/S). Choosing ε=Θ⁡(min⁡{1,S/T})\varepsilon=\Theta(\min\{1,\sqrt{S/T}\}) with a sufficiently small constant keeps the probability that y^i​j≠θi​j\widehat{y}_{ij}\neq\theta_{ij} bounded below by a constant in every round, averaged over a uniformly random sign vector 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}. Summing the resulting losses over all SS signs and TT rounds yields regret Ω⁡(min⁡{T,S​T})\Omega(\min\{T,\sqrt{ST}\}) for some fixed sign vector. In the SOO instance, the policy chooses the prediction vector at the root and then observes all coordinates in order, and we order the 2​si+12s_{i}+1 values of coordinate ii such that every optimistic continuation value has level-set complexity at most sis_{i}.

1.3 Related Work

For known distributions, prophet inequalities provide guarantees against the expected offline optimum for a single selection [26], multiple selections [1], and matroid constraints [25]. Approximation algorithms are also known for many stochastic combinatorial optimization problems [10, 30, 2, 20].

In combinatorial bandits [8], the learner selects a set of arms and observes each of them, and algorithms based on upper confidence bounds achieve O~​(m​n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{mnT}) regret for linear rewards when at most mm arms are selected [27]. Extensions allow rewards that depend on the whole distributions of the arms [6] and additional arms that are revealed depending on the outcomes [7]. In our setting, the policy also adapts its actions to the values observed within a round.

SOO can also be cast as an episodic Markov decision process (MDP) whose states are observation histories. Our algorithm resembles optimistic planning over a set of plausible transition models, as in extended value iteration [23], and our variance analysis resembles the use of the law of total variance in the upper confidence bound value iteration algorithm [3]. However, regret bounds for tabular MDPs depend on the numbers of states and actions, and observation histories can be exponentially many in nn, or infinitely many for continuous observations. Factored MDPs [36] exploit a product structure of the transitions, but their bounds still depend on the sizes of the factored state spaces. In SOO, all histories share the same coordinate distributions, and the level-set condition on the optimistic continuation values removes the dependence on the numbers of histories and support points.

Other work on learning in SOO considers specific problems. Gatmiry, Kesselheim, Singla, and Wang [14] proved an O~​(n3​T)\widetilde{O}(n^{3}\sqrt{T}) upper bound and an Ω⁡(T)\Omega(\sqrt{T}) lower bound for the prophet inequality under bandit feedback. Liu, Chen, Wang, Luo, and Ratliff [29] obtained O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}) for the prophet inequality and Pandora’s box under semi-bandit feedback by using problem-specific structure. For Pandora’s box with inspection costs cic_{i} and values in [0,1][0,1], their bound avoids the factor 1+∑ici1+\sum_{i}c_{i} introduced by normalizing the net reward in our general bound.

A related line of work studies the sample complexity of stochastic optimization, with bounds for single-parameter revenue maximization [18], the prophet inequality [9], and general problems over product distributions [17]. For the last class, Guo, Huang, Tang, and Zhang [17] show that O~​(n​k/ε2)\widetilde{O}(nk/\varepsilon^{2}) samples suffice for supports of size at most kk. Under a stronger monotonicity condition, O~​(n/ε2)\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^{2}) samples suffice, and both bounds are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Under full feedback, such bounds lead to regret with T\sqrt{T} dependence, whereas under semi-bandit feedback, an explore-then-commit approach typically leads to T2/3T^{2/3} dependence [15].

In concurrent and independent work that appeared on arXiv shortly before this submission, Zhuo and Nagarajan [39] and Hu and Ghuge [22] improved the regret bounds for FSD-monotone problems.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Model

Let ℤ>0\mathbb{Z}_{>0} be the set of positive integers. For m∈ℤ>0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, write [m]={1,…,m}[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}, and for a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, write a+=max⁡{a,0}a_{+}=\max\{a,0\}. Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be independent random variables with unknown distributions D1,…,DnD_{1},\ldots,D_{n}, and write D=∏i=1nDiD=\prod_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}. Each XiX_{i} takes values in a known subset of [0,1][0,1], called its domain (e.g., {0,1}\{0,1\} or [0,1][0,1]). Our algorithm and analysis use only the order of the values, and hence real-valued coordinates can be mapped into [0,1][0,1] by a known strictly increasing function. We refer to XiX_{i} as coordinate ii and say that coordinate ii is revealed when its realized value is observed.

A problem is specified by a finite rooted directed tree (V,A)(V,A), called the decision tree,11 1 The analysis applies, with subtrees replaced by the subgraphs reachable from a node, to a finite directed acyclic graph with a single root in which all paths from the root to each node reveal the same coordinates, and hence obs⁡(u)\mathrm{obs}(u) below is well defined. Such a graph can be much smaller than the corresponding tree, as in SBFE, where a node can represent the set of tested coordinates. We use trees for simplicity. with root rr and children ch⁡(u)\mathrm{ch}(u) at node uu, together with the observation sets, feasible actions, and leaf rewards defined below. The set obs⁡(u)⊆[n]\mathrm{obs}(u)\subseteq[n] contains the coordinates already observed upon reaching uu, and xobs⁡(u)=(xi)i∈obs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}=(x_{i})_{i\in\mathrm{obs}(u)} denotes their values. The coordinates in obs⁡(r)\mathrm{obs}(r) are observed before the first action. Each edge (u,v)(u,v) is either a revelation edge, which reveals one new coordinate ii, with obs⁡(v)=obs⁡(u)∪{i}\mathrm{obs}(v)=\mathrm{obs}(u)\cup\{i\} and i∉obs⁡(u)i\notin\mathrm{obs}(u), or a stopping edge, which leads to a leaf vv without a new observation, with obs⁡(v)=obs⁡(u)\mathrm{obs}(v)=\mathrm{obs}(u). Thus, a coordinate is observed at most once per round. We remark that an action that reveals several coordinates at once can be represented by a chain of revelation edges with no intermediate choices. A revelation edge may also lead to a leaf.

We regard each child of a node as an action at that node, and at a non-leaf node uu with observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}, the feasible actions form a nonempty set 𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))⊆ch⁡(u)\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})\subseteq\mathrm{ch}(u). A leaf ℓ\ell has reward fℓ​(xobs⁡(ℓ))∈[0,1]f_{\ell}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(\ell)})\in[0,1]. The tree encodes only the actions and the order of observations, and the observed values are carried along as xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}. In the example of Figure 1, a single node u12u_{12} serves all pairs (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}), and its feasible actions depend on whether x1=x2x_{1}=x_{2}. Reward functions and functions specifying feasibility are assumed to be measurable.

A deterministic policy σ\sigma chooses a feasible action σu​(xobs⁡(u))∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))\sigma_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) at each non-leaf node uu. Deterministic policies are assumed to be measurable, and a randomized policy is a distribution over them. For a policy σ\sigma and a realization xx, write f⁡(σ,x)f(\sigma,x) for the reward, averaged over the randomness of σ\sigma, and let

f⁡(σ∣D)=𝔼X∼D​[f⁡(σ,X)],OPT⁡(D)=supσf⁡(σ∣D).f(\sigma\mid D)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim D}[f(\sigma,X)],\qquad\mathrm{OPT}(D)=\sup_{\sigma}f(\sigma\mid D).

The learner faces the same problem in each of TT rounds. Before the first round, the learner knows the problem and TT, but not DD. In each round t∈[T]t\in[T], a vector Xt∼DX^{t}\sim D is drawn independently of the previous rounds. The learner chooses a policy σt\sigma^{t} based on the observations from the previous rounds and possibly internal randomness, and σt\sigma^{t} adapts to the observations within round tt. If ℓt\ell^{t} is the leaf reached, the learner observes Xobs⁡(ℓt)tX^{t}_{\mathrm{obs}(\ell^{t})}, which we call semi-bandit feedback. Let Ni,tN_{i,t} be the number of rounds before round tt in which coordinate ii was revealed, and let Zi,1,…,Zi,Ni,tZ_{i,1},\ldots,Z_{i,N_{i,t}} be the revealed values in order.

The expected regret of the policy σt\sigma^{t} chosen in round tt is Regt=OPT⁡(D)−f⁡(σt∣D)\mathrm{Reg}_{t}=\mathrm{OPT}(D)-f(\sigma^{t}\mid D). Taking expectation over the past observations and the learner’s randomness, we define the cumulative expected regret as

RT=∑t=1T𝔼⁡[Regt]=∑t=1T(OPT⁡(D)−𝔼⁡[f⁡(σt,Xt)]).R_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Reg}_{t}]=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(\mathrm{OPT}(D)-\mathbb{E}[f(\sigma^{t},X^{t})]\bigr).

We write RT​(D)R_{T}(D) when the dependence on DD matters. The benchmark OPT⁡(D)\mathrm{OPT}(D) is attained by a policy that knows DD but, like the learner, observes the coordinates only along its execution path. For α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1], we also define the cumulative expected α\alpha-regret as

RT(α)=∑t=1T(α​OPT​(D)−𝔼⁡[f⁡(σt,Xt)]).R_{T}^{(\alpha)}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(D)-\mathbb{E}[f(\sigma^{t},X^{t})]\bigr).

We define functions gug_{u} and h(u,v)h_{(u,v)} by backward induction. At a leaf, gℓ=fℓg_{\ell}=f_{\ell}. At a non-leaf node,

gu​(xobs⁡(u))\displaystyle g_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) =maxv∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))⁡h(u,v)​(xobs⁡(u)),\displaystyle=\textstyle\max_{v\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})}h_{(u,v)}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), (2.1)
h(u,v)​(xobs⁡(u))\displaystyle h_{(u,v)}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) ={𝔼Xi∼Di​[gv​(Xi,xobs⁡(u))],if ​obs​(v)∖obs⁡(u)={i},fv​(xobs⁡(u)),if ​obs​(v)=obs⁡(u).\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}_{X_{i}\sim D_{i}}[g_{v}(X_{i},x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})],&\text{if }\mathrm{obs}(v)\setminus\mathrm{obs}(u)=\{i\},\\ f_{v}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}),&\text{if }\mathrm{obs}(v)=\mathrm{obs}(u).\end{cases} (2.2)

Here, (xi,xobs⁡(u))(x_{i},x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) adds the value of coordinate ii to the observations, with coordinates identified by their indices. We call gu​(xobs⁡(u))g_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) the optimal continuation value at uu. It is the maximum expected reward obtainable after reaching uu with observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}, and h(u,v)​(xobs⁡(u))h_{(u,v)}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) is the corresponding maximum when the next move is to vv. By backward induction, choosing a maximizing child at every node is optimal, and

OPT⁡(D)=𝔼Xobs⁡(r)∼∏i∈obs⁡(r)Di​[gr​(Xobs⁡(r))].\mathrm{OPT}(D)=\mathbb{E}_{X_{\mathrm{obs}(r)}\sim\prod_{i\in\mathrm{obs}(r)}D_{i}}[g_{r}(X_{\mathrm{obs}(r)})]. (2.3)

We now relate our model to that of Ghuge, Zhuo, Agarwal, and Nagarajan [15]. They describe a policy as a tree whose internal nodes are labeled by the coordinates to observe next and whose branches correspond to the observed values. When the constraints on policies are imposed on each path, such a problem fits our model, with the nodes of (V,A)(V,A) corresponding to the sequences of observed coordinates. For continuous distributions, they consider policies with finitely many threshold branches at each node, since an arbitrary policy can have uncountably many branches. In our applications, an optimal policy can depend on the exact observed values, for example, through the maximum of the past values in optimal stopping with loss aversion, and it may then need uncountably many branches in their model. Our model carries the observed values along a finite tree, and a policy chooses a child at each node by a measurable function of these values. Carrying the values also makes each continuation value, such as gv​(⋅,xobs⁡(u))g_{v}(\cdot,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), a function of the coordinate revealed on the edge (u,v)(u,v), and our regret bounds depend on the level-set complexity of such functions (Section 3).

2.2 Monotonicity and Level-Set Complexity

For distributions P,QP,Q, we say that PP first-order stochastically dominates (FSD) QQ if P⁡([0,x])≤Q⁡([0,x])P([0,x])\leq Q([0,x]) for all x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]. A problem is FSD-monotone [15] if either OPT⁡(D)≤OPT⁡(E)\mathrm{OPT}(D)\leq\mathrm{OPT}(E) for all product distributions D=∏iDiD=\prod_{i}D_{i} and E=∏iEiE=\prod_{i}E_{i} such that EiE_{i} dominates DiD_{i} for every ii, or OPT⁡(D)≥OPT⁡(E)\mathrm{OPT}(D)\geq\mathrm{OPT}(E) for all such DD and EE. A problem is realization-monotone if the leaf rewards and the sets of feasible actions are all nondecreasing in every observed value, or all nonincreasing in every observed value, with the other values fixed and sets ordered by inclusion. If, for each coordinate ii, the leaf rewards and the sets of feasible actions are monotone in xix_{i} in a direction that depends on ii, reversing the order of the values of the coordinates with the nonincreasing direction, which affects neither the algorithm nor level-set complexity, makes the problem realization-monotone. Realization monotonicity implies FSD monotonicity, since expectations and maxima over sets of feasible actions that are monotone in the same direction preserve monotonicity, and hence backward induction shows that every continuation value is monotone in each observed value and that the optimal value is monotone in each distribution. The converse fails, since FSD monotonicity concerns only the optimal value. For example, if the root has a stopping edge to a leaf with reward 1 and an edge revealing X1X_{1} to a leaf with reward ψ⁡(x1)∈[0,1]\psi(x_{1})\in[0,1], the optimal value is always 1, whereas ψ\psi need not be monotone and can have any level-set complexity.

For an integer s≥1s\geq 1, let ℐs\mathcal{I}_{s} be the family of unions of at most ss intervals in [0,1][0,1], including the empty set. Intervals may be open, closed, half-open, or singletons. A function ϕ\phi on a subset of [0,1][0,1] has level-set complexity at most ss if, for every y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}, there exists B∈ℐsB\in\mathcal{I}_{s} such that the superlevel set of ϕ\phi at yy satisfies

{z∈dom⁡(ϕ):ϕ⁡(z)>y}=dom⁡(ϕ)∩B.\{z\in\operatorname{dom}(\phi):\phi(z)>y\}=\operatorname{dom}(\phi)\cap B.

By convention, every function has level-set complexity at most ∞\infty.

A function has level-set complexity at most 1 if it is monotone or unimodal, that is, nondecreasing and then nonincreasing. A function has level-set complexity at most 2 if it is nonincreasing and then nondecreasing, for example, the maximum of a nondecreasing function and a nonincreasing function, since each superlevel set is then the intersection of the domain with the complement of an interval. When the domain is an interval, the same bounds hold for quasi-concave and quasi-convex functions, respectively. A function on a domain of at most kk points has level-set complexity at most ⌈k/2⌉\lceil k/2\rceil, since each superlevel set consists of at most that many runs of consecutive domain points.

3 Main Results

We present an optimistic DP algorithm and state regret bounds in terms of level-set complexity, together with a worst-case lower bound that matches the main upper bound up to logarithmic factors. We then extend the upper bound to problems whose reward decomposes into the reward earned so far and the future reward, such as scheduling and overbooking.

3.1 Optimistic Dynamic Programming

At the beginning of each round, the algorithm forms a confidence set of distributions for each coordinate from the samples collected so far. It then evaluates the DP defined by (2.1) and (2.2) with each expectation replaced by its supremum over the corresponding confidence set, and during the round it chooses, at each node, a child that maximizes the resulting optimistic value.

For each m≥1m\geq 1, write D^i,m\widehat{D}_{i,m} for the empirical distribution of the first mm revealed values Zi,1,…,Zi,mZ_{i,1},\ldots,Z_{i,m} of coordinate ii, that is, D^i,m(B)=1m∑j=1m𝟏{Zi,j∈B}\widehat{D}_{i,m}(B)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\{Z_{i,j}\in B\} for B⊆[0,1]B\subseteq[0,1]. For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), let

Λ=log⁡(80​n​(T+1)3/δ).\Lambda=\log\left({80n(T+1)^{3}}/{\delta}\right).

For m≥1m\geq 1 and z∈[0,1]z\in[0,1], define

bm​(z)=min⁡{1, 6​z⁡(1−z)​Λ/m+32​Λ/m}.b_{m}(z)=\min\left\{1,\;6\sqrt{z(1-z)\Lambda/m}+32\Lambda/m\right\}. (3.1)

The confidence set for m≥1m\geq 1 observations of coordinate ii is

𝒞m(D^i,m)={Q:|Q(I)−D^i,m(I)|≤bm(D^i,m(I))∀I∈ℐ1},\mathcal{C}_{m}(\widehat{D}_{i,m})=\left\{Q:|Q(I)-\widehat{D}_{i,m}(I)|\leq b_{m}(\widehat{D}_{i,m}(I))\quad\forall I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\right\}, (3.2)

where QQ ranges over distributions on the coordinate’s domain. For m=0m=0, let D^i,0\widehat{D}_{i,0} be an arbitrary fixed distribution on the coordinate’s domain and let 𝒞0​(D^i,0)\mathcal{C}_{0}(\widehat{D}_{i,0}) be the set of all distributions on that domain. For m≥1m\geq 1, the empirical distribution belongs to the confidence set, and hence the set is always nonempty. For m≤32​Λm\leq 32\Lambda, we have bm≡1b_{m}\equiv 1, and the confidence set consists of all distributions on the coordinate’s domain.

At the beginning of round tt, set 𝒞i,t=𝒞Ni,t​(D^i,Ni,t)\mathcal{C}_{i,t}=\mathcal{C}_{N_{i,t}}(\widehat{D}_{i,N_{i,t}}). These sets stay fixed throughout the round. Define g¯ℓt=fℓ\bar{g}_{\ell}^{\,t}=f_{\ell} at leaves and

g¯ut​(xobs⁡(u))\displaystyle\bar{g}_{u}^{\,t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) =maxv∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))⁡h¯(u,v)t​(xobs⁡(u)),\displaystyle=\max\nolimits_{v\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})}\bar{h}_{(u,v)}^{\,t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), (3.3)
h¯(u,v)t​(xobs⁡(u))\displaystyle\bar{h}_{(u,v)}^{\,t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) ={supQ∈𝒞i,t𝔼Xi∼Q​[g¯vt​(Xi,xobs⁡(u))],if ​obs​(v)∖obs⁡(u)={i},fv​(xobs⁡(u)),if ​obs​(v)=obs⁡(u).\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}\mathbb{E}_{X_{i}\sim Q}[\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t}(X_{i},x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})],&\text{if }\mathrm{obs}(v)\setminus\mathrm{obs}(u)=\{i\},\\ f_{v}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}),&\text{if }\mathrm{obs}(v)=\mathrm{obs}(u).\end{cases} (3.4)

We call g¯ut​(xobs⁡(u))\bar{g}_{u}^{\,t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) the optimistic continuation value at uu. The suprema at different edges may be attained by different distributions, and no single product distribution needs to attain all optimistic values. Upon reaching node uu, the algorithm chooses

σut​(xobs⁡(u))∈arg​maxv∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))⁡h¯(u,v)t​(xobs⁡(u)),\textstyle\sigma_{u}^{t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{v\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})}\bar{h}_{(u,v)}^{\,t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), (3.5)

breaking ties in a fixed order. Appendix A shows that each supremum in (3.4) is the optimal value of an LP whose size is polynomial in the number of samples, given the suprema of g¯vt\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t} over the cells formed by the sample points and the intervals between them. For infinite domains, we assume that the optimistic values are measurable in the samples and observations, which makes this policy measurable. This holds automatically for finite domains. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

3.2 Regret Bounds

The regret depends on how the optimistic continuation values vary with the coordinate revealed next. On an edge (u,v)(u,v) that reveals coordinate ii, the optimistic value h¯(u,v)t\bar{h}_{(u,v)}^{\,t} is the supremum of the expectation of z↦g¯vt​(z,xobs⁡(u))z\mapsto\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) over 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t}, as defined in (3.4). We bound the difference between this optimistic value and the expectation of the same continuation-value function under DiD_{i}. Since expectations can be expressed as integrals of superlevel-set probabilities, the interval constraints control this difference whenever Di∈𝒞i,tD_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t} and each superlevel set is a union of a few intervals. We assume the following bound on the level-set complexity of this function for any confidence sets.

Assumption 3.1.

There are s1,…,sn∈ℤ>0∪{∞}s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\} with the following property. Let 𝒫1,…,𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{n} be any nonempty sets of distributions on the domains of the coordinates, and let g¯\bar{g} be defined by (3.3) and (3.4) with 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} in place of 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t}. Then, for every edge (u,v)(u,v) revealing coordinate ii and all observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)} for which v∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))v\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), the function z↦g¯v​(z,xobs⁡(u))z\mapsto\bar{g}_{v}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) has level-set complexity at most sis_{i}.

We can take si=1s_{i}=1 for every coordinate if the problem is realization-monotone, since the backward induction in Section 2.2, which also applies to suprema, shows that every optimistic continuation value is then monotone. These parameters are small constants in many problems, including SBFE, the full-information secretary problem, and optimal stopping with loss aversion in Section 4. If the domain of coordinate ii is finite, the assumption holds with sis_{i} equal to half its size rounded up, which is 1 for binary coordinates. The assumption always holds with si=∞s_{i}=\infty, for which it imposes no condition on coordinate ii.

The following theorem bounds the regret in terms of these complexities and the support sizes.

Theorem 3.2.

Under Assumption 3.1, let ki∈ℤ>0∪{∞}k_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\} be the number of support points of DiD_{i}, and suppose that S=∑i=1nmin⁡{si,ki}S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{s_{i},k_{i}\} is finite. There is a universal constant cc such that, for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), Algorithm 1 satisfies

RT≤c⁡(S​T​Λ​log⁡T​(1+log⁡T)+S​Λ​(1+log⁡T))+δ​T.R_{T}\leq c\bigl(\sqrt{ST\Lambda\log T(1+\log T)}+S\Lambda(1+\log T)\bigr)+\delta T. (3.6)

In particular, for δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1), we have RT=O~​(S​T)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST}).

The last statement holds because δ​T<1\delta T<1 and S≤S​TS\leq\sqrt{ST} when T≥ST\geq S, whereas RT≤T≤S​TR_{T}\leq T\leq\sqrt{ST} when T<ST<S. Algorithm 1 requires no knowledge of sis_{i} or kik_{i}, adapts to the smaller of the two for each coordinate, and uses TT only through Λ\Lambda. For unknown TT, the doubling trick, restarting the algorithm in phases of lengths H=2jH=2^{j} for j=0,1,…j=0,1,\ldots with HH in place of TT and δ=1/(H+1)\delta=1/(H+1), yields RT=O~​(S​T)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST}) for every TT.

Since Assumption 3.1 holds with si=∞s_{i}=\infty, Theorem 3.2 yields the following corollary, which bounds the regret in terms of the support sizes even when the supports are unknown.

Corollary 3.3.

Suppose that each distribution DiD_{i} has at most kik_{i} support points, and let K=k1+⋯+knK=k_{1}+\cdots+k_{n}. Then, for δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1), Algorithm 1 satisfies RT=O~​(K​T)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT}), without any condition on the level-set complexity.

If the supports were known, we could restrict the coordinate domains to them and apply Theorem 3.2 with si=⌈ki/2⌉s_{i}=\lceil k_{i}/2\rceil. Corollary 3.3 requires neither the supports nor their sizes as input and allows infinite coordinate domains. Restricting the continuation-value functions to the true supports does not suffice, since distributions in the confidence sets may place mass outside these supports, and the proof of Theorem 3.2 accounts for this mass through Lemma 5.5.

The analysis also applies to algorithms that choose a single product distribution from the confidence sets, provided that its optimal value is at least the true one up to 1/T1/T. For a product distribution P=∏iPiP=\prod_{i}P_{i}, let gPg^{P} and hPh^{P} be defined by (2.1) and (2.2) with PiP_{i} in place of DiD_{i}. A policy is optimal for PP at every node if, at every non-leaf node and for all observations, it chooses a child that maximizes hPh^{P}.

Proposition 3.4.

Suppose obs⁡(r)=∅\mathrm{obs}(r)=\emptyset and let δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1). For each round tt, let Qt=∏iQitQ^{t}=\prod_{i}Q_{i}^{t} be a product distribution determined by the observations before round tt, with Qit∈𝒞i,tQ_{i}^{t}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t} for every ii, and satisfying OPT⁡(Qt)≥OPT⁡(D)−1/T\mathrm{OPT}(Q^{t})\geq\mathrm{OPT}(D)-1/T whenever Di∈𝒞i,tD_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t} for every ii.

  1. (a)

    Suppose that, for every product distribution PP, every edge (u,v)(u,v) revealing a coordinate ii, and all observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)} for which v∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))v\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), the function z↦gvP​(z,xobs⁡(u))z\mapsto g_{v}^{P}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) has level-set complexity at most sis_{i}, and let SS be as in Theorem 3.2. If the algorithm runs a policy that is optimal for QtQ^{t} at every node, then RT=O~​(S​T)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST}).

  2. (b)

    Let α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1], suppose that each DiD_{i} has at most kik_{i} support points, and let K=k1+⋯+knK=k_{1}+\cdots+k_{n}. If the algorithm runs a policy σt\sigma^{t} with f⁡(σt∣Qt)≥α​OPT​(Qt)f(\sigma^{t}\mid Q^{t})\geq\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(Q^{t}), then RT(α)≤O~​(K​T)R_{T}^{(\alpha)}\leq\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT}).

The condition obs⁡(r)=∅\mathrm{obs}(r)=\emptyset can be satisfied by adding dummy nodes before the original root and revealing the initial observations along the resulting chain of edges. Thus, it does not restrict the SOO problems that can be represented.

A distribution QtQ^{t} that satisfies the conditions in the proposition always exists, although finding it can be difficult in general. For example, it can be computed when every domain is finite and the optimal value is nondecreasing under FSD. For each ii, we can solve an LP to find a distribution Qit∈𝒞i,tQ_{i}^{t}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t} that stochastically dominates every distribution in 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} (Lemma A.2). Then Qt=∏iQitQ^{t}=\prod_{i}Q_{i}^{t} satisfies OPT⁡(Qt)≥OPT⁡(D)\mathrm{OPT}(Q^{t})\geq\mathrm{OPT}(D) whenever Di∈𝒞i,tD_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t} for every ii.

Part (b) shows that, if an α\alpha-approximation policy is known for the underlying SOO problem with known distributions, we can incorporate it into this approach, as in the algorithm of Ghuge, Zhuo, Agarwal, and Nagarajan [15]. The resulting α\alpha-regret is O~​(K​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT}).

The variance bound in the proof of Theorem 3.2 can be refined to depend on the optimal value.

Proposition 3.5.

Under Assumption 3.1, let SS be as in Theorem 3.2 and p=OPT⁡(D)p=\mathrm{OPT}(D). For δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1), Algorithm 1 satisfies RT=O~​(S​T​p​(1−p)+S)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST\,p(1-p)}+S).

This bound is smaller than that of Theorem 3.2 when the optimal value is close to 0 or 1. Section 5.2 proves Theorem 3.2 and Propositions 3.4 and 3.5, using the confidence-set bounds from Section 5.1.

The next theorem shows that, up to logarithmic factors, the dependence on SS and TT in Theorem 3.2 is necessary, even under full feedback.

Theorem 3.6.

For any integers T≥1T\geq 1 and s1,…,sn≥1s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\geq 1, there is a problem with nn coordinates that has the following properties.

  1. (i)

    Every coordinate has a finite domain, and every leaf reward is 0 or 1. The learner receives full feedback, that is, all nn coordinates are observed in every round under every policy.

  2. (ii)

    Assumption 3.1 holds with s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n}.

  3. (iii)

    For every randomized learning algorithm, there is a product distribution DD for which RT​(D)≥164​min⁡{T,S​T}R_{T}(D)\geq\frac{1}{64}\min\{T,\sqrt{ST}\}, where S=s1+⋯+snS=s_{1}+\cdots+s_{n} and each DiD_{i} has 2​si+12s_{i}+1 support points.

The proof is in Section 6. Together with Theorem 3.2, it shows that the worst-case regret over the problems satisfying Assumption 3.1 with s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n} is Θ~​(min⁡{T,S​T})\widetilde{\Theta}(\min\{T,\sqrt{ST}\}) for S=∑isiS=\sum_{i}s_{i}. Since coordinate ii of this instance has 2​si+12s_{i}+1 support points, the bound of Corollary 3.3 is also tight up to logarithmic factors in the worst case over supports of these sizes. The lower-bound instance has 2S2^{S} root actions, and the rate S​T\sqrt{ST} coincides with the rate T​log⁡2S\sqrt{T\log 2^{S}} of prediction with expert advice over 2S2^{S} actions under full feedback [5]. The number of actions does not affect the upper bound, since Theorem 3.2 does not depend on the size of the tree.

3.3 Extension to Immediate Rewards

In some applications, the continuation value decomposes into an immediate reward and a residual value. Their sum can have large level-set complexity even when each term has small complexity. For example, in overbooking with group reservations, the refund savings of a group are nondecreasing and the remaining net revenue is nonincreasing in its show-up count, but the optimistic continuation value can alternate between two values as this count increases (Section 4.5). The following theorem bounds the regret by controlling the expectation errors of the two terms separately. We assume that the immediate rewards are nonnegative and sum to at most 1 along each root-to-leaf path consisting of feasible actions. We also require that increasing the revealed value, with all other values fixed, cannot increase the residual reward or enlarge the set of feasible actions at any subsequent node.

Theorem 3.7.

Let s1,…,sn≥1s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\geq 1 be integers and S=∑isiS=\sum_{i}s_{i}. Suppose that each revelation edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) has a measurable immediate reward χe​(xobs⁡(v))∈[0,1]\chi_{e}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(v)})\in[0,1] satisfying the following conditions.

  1. (a)

    For every edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) revealing ii, fix any xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)} for which v∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))v\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}). The function χe​(⋅,xobs⁡(u))\chi_{e}(\cdot,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) has level-set complexity at most sis_{i}, and every leaf ℓ\ell in the subtree rooted at vv admits the decomposition

    fℓ​(xobs⁡(ℓ))=κe​(xobs⁡(u))+χe​(xobs⁡(v))+Fe,ℓ​(xobs⁡(ℓ)),0≤Fe,ℓ≤1,f_{\ell}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(\ell)})=\kappa_{e}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})+\chi_{e}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(v)})+F_{e,\ell}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(\ell)}),\qquad 0\leq F_{e,\ell}\leq 1,

    where κe\kappa_{e} is common to all such leaves and the identity holds for all remaining coordinate values.

  2. (b)

    For each edge and fixed observations in (a), the residual rewards Fe,ℓF_{e,\ell} and the sets of feasible actions in the subtree rooted at vv are nonincreasing in xix_{i}, with other coordinates fixed and sets ordered by inclusion.

  3. (c)

    The immediate rewards sum to at most 1 along every root-to-leaf path consisting of feasible actions.

Then, for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), Algorithm 1 satisfies (3.6) with a larger universal constant cc. In particular, for δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1), we have RT=O~​(S​T)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST}).

Since the supremum of a sum is at most the sum of the suprema, the proof bounds the expectation errors separately for the immediate reward and the residual continuation value, and hence no level-set bound on their sum is needed. As in Theorem 3.2, the bound also holds with S=∑imin⁡{si,ki}S=\sum_{i}\min\{s_{i},k_{i}\}, since Lemma 5.5 applies to the immediate rewards if ki<sik_{i}<s_{i}.

When the total immediate reward is bounded by the leaf reward, the regret bound can be refined in terms of the optimal value.

Proposition 3.8.

In addition to the conditions of Theorem 3.7, suppose that the sum in (c) is at most the reward of the leaf at the end of the path, and let p=OPT⁡(D)p=\mathrm{OPT}(D). For δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1), Algorithm 1 satisfies RT=O~​(S​T​p+S)R_{T}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{STp}+S).

Section 5.3 proves Theorem 3.7 and Proposition 3.8.

4 Applications

We apply Theorems 3.2 and 3.7 to five problems, none of which is FSD-monotone in general. In each problem, the objective lies in a known interval of length Γ>0\Gamma>0. We rescale it to a reward in [0,1][0,1] by an affine map. For cost minimization, the reward is 1 minus the incurred cost divided by Γ\Gamma. Regret in the original objective is then Γ\Gamma times the normalized regret. Throughout this section, we take δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1). When the scheduling reward functions have bounded level-set complexity, all five problems admit regret O~​(Γ​n​T)\widetilde{O}(\Gamma\sqrt{nT}) in the original objective, and Table 2 lists sharper bounds that depend on the optimal values.

4.1 Stochastic Boolean Function Evaluation

In SBFE, a known Boolean function F:{0,1}n→{0,1}F:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} and nonnegative testing costs c1,…,cnc_{1},\ldots,c_{n} are given, and the success probabilities of the independent binary variables XiX_{i} are unknown. A policy tests coordinates one at a time until the observed values determine F⁡(X)F(X), that is, until all completions of the unobserved coordinates yield the same function value. The objective is to minimize the expected testing cost. SBFE is a basic model of sequential testing, and approximation algorithms for known probabilities have been studied [12].

Each node of the tree corresponds to the sequence of coordinates tested so far. If the observed values do not determine FF, the feasible actions are the tests of the untested coordinates. Otherwise, the policy stops. With Γ=∑ici>0\Gamma=\sum_{i}c_{i}>0, the reward at a leaf ℓ\ell is fℓ=1−(∑i∈obs⁡(ℓ)ci)/Γf_{\ell}=1-(\sum_{i\in\mathrm{obs}(\ell)}c_{i})/\Gamma.

To see that SBFE need not be FSD-monotone, consider the majority function of three variables with unit testing costs shown in Figure 1, and suppose that all three variables have a common success probability p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1). At least two tests are required, and the third is needed exactly when the first two outcomes differ. By symmetry, regardless of the order, the optimal expected cost is 2+2​p​(1−p)2+2p(1-p). For p=1/4,1/2,3/4p=1/4,1/2,3/4, the Bernoulli distribution increases in FSD, while the cost is 19/819/8, 5/25/2, and 19/819/8. Thus, the problem is not FSD-monotone, although the majority function is monotone as a Boolean function.

Proposition 4.1.

For SBFE with any Boolean function and nonnegative testing costs, the expected regret in the original testing cost is O~​(Γ​n​T)\widetilde{O}(\Gamma\sqrt{nT}).

Proof.

Every coordinate is binary, and hence Assumption 3.1 holds with si=1s_{i}=1 for every ii, as noted after the assumption. Theorem 3.2 with S=nS=n implies the claim. ∎

Let C∗C^{*} be the optimal expected testing cost. Since the optimal normalized reward is 1−C∗/Γ1-C^{*}/\Gamma, Proposition 3.5 bounds the regret in the original testing cost also by O~​(n​T​C∗​(Γ−C∗)+Γ​n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT\,C^{*}(\Gamma-C^{*})}+\Gamma n), which is smaller when C∗≪ΓC^{*}\ll\Gamma. For threshold functions F(x)=𝟏{x1+⋯+xn≥θ}F(x)=\mathbf{1}\{x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n}\geq\theta\}, which include the majority function, the reward splits into two parts that are FSD-monotone in opposite directions, and a variant of the classical optimal policy for known distributions [4, 33] is optimal for both parts under different optimistic distributions. Applying Proposition 3.4 to each part yields an algorithm with O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) time per round and regret O~​(Γ​n​T)\widetilde{O}(\Gamma\sqrt{nT}) (Proposition B.1 in Appendix B).

4.2 Full-Information Secretary Problem

In the full-information secretary problem, candidates with independent values X1,…,Xn∈[0,1]X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\in[0,1] arrive in this order, the decision maker decides immediately whether to accept the current candidate, and the goal is to maximize the probability of accepting a candidate with the largest value among all nn candidates. Unlike in the classical secretary problem, the decision maker observes the values themselves rather than only their relative ranks. Gilbert and Mosteller [16] study identical known distributions, and Esfandiari, Hajiaghayi, Lucier, and Mitzenmacher [13] study non-identical known distributions. Harada, Kawase, and Sumita [21] study the repeated version with unknown distributions under full feedback, together with per-round guarantees relative to a baseline. Since leaf rewards depend only on revealed values and the success of a policy depends on the values after the accepted candidate, these values must be revealed after acceptance, and hence all values are observed in every round.

Let uiu_{i} be the node at time ii, with X1X_{1} initially observed at the root r=u1r=u_{1}. For i<ni<n, the node uiu_{i} has a child ui+1u_{i+1} revealing Xi+1X_{i+1} and another child that starts a chain of revelation edges revealing Xi+1,…,XnX_{i+1},\ldots,X_{n} in order with no intermediate choices and ending at a leaf ℓi\ell_{i}, and un=ℓnu_{n}=\ell_{n} is the final leaf. The reward at ℓi\ell_{i} is fℓi(x)=𝟏{xi≥xj for all j∈[n]}f_{\ell_{i}}(x)=\mathbf{1}\{x_{i}\geq x_{j}\text{ for all }j\in[n]\}, and hence Γ=1\Gamma=1.

The problem is not FSD-monotone even with two candidates. Let n=2n=2, X1=1/2X_{1}=1/2, and X2∈{0,1}X_{2}\in\{0,1\} with ℙ⁡(X2=1)=q\mathbb{P}(X_{2}=1)=q. Accepting the first candidate succeeds with probability 1−q1-q, and accepting the second succeeds with probability qq. Hence, the optimal success probability is max⁡{q,1−q}\max\{q,1-q\}, which first decreases and then increases as qq increases.

Proposition 4.2.

For the full-information secretary problem, Assumption 3.1 holds with s1=⋯=sn=2s_{1}=\cdots=s_{n}=2, and the expected regret is O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}).

Proof.

Fix arbitrary nonempty sets of distributions as in Assumption 3.1. Every leaf reward is nondecreasing in the value of the accepted candidate and nonincreasing in the values of the other candidates, and the feasible actions do not depend on the values. Expectations, suprema, and maxima preserve these monotonicities. Hence, backward induction shows that every optimistic continuation value on the chain after accepting candidate ii is nondecreasing in xix_{i} and nonincreasing in the values of the other candidates, and that the optimistic continuation value at uku_{k} is nonincreasing in each past value xjx_{j} with j<kj<k. The optimistic continuation value after a value is revealed on a chain is therefore monotone in that value. At uiu_{i} with i<ni<n, the value of accepting is nondecreasing in xix_{i}, and the value of continuing is nonincreasing in xix_{i}. Their maximum has level-set complexity at most 2, and the value at unu_{n} is nondecreasing in xnx_{n}. Thus, Assumption 3.1 holds with si=2s_{i}=2, and Theorem 3.2 with S≤2​nS\leq 2n implies the claim. ∎

Proposition 3.5 refines the bound to O~​(n​T​p∗​(1−p∗)+n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})}+n), where p∗p^{*} is the optimal success probability, and this bound is smaller when p∗p^{*} is close to 0 or 1. If every domain is finite, Proposition A.4 applies with the following states. At uiu_{i}, the state is the pair of maxj<i⁡xj\max_{j<i}x_{j}, which is 0 for i=1i=1, and xix_{i}. On the chain after accepting candidate ii, the state is the pair of xix_{i} and the indicator that xix_{i} is at least every value revealed so far. Each round then runs in time polynomial in nn, tt, and the sizes of the domains.

The model also captures random arrival orders. For k∈[n−1]k\in[n-1], let YkY_{k} be an additional coordinate with the uniform distribution on [0,1][0,1]. Before the kkth arrival, that is, at the root if k=1k=1 and after the rejection of the (k−1)(k-1)th arriving candidate otherwise, the next edge reveals YkY_{k}. The only feasible action then reveals the candidate selected by YkY_{k} through the conditional distribution of the kkth arrival given the previous arrivals, for example, by listing the remaining candidates in a fixed order and selecting the first one whose cumulative conditional probability is at least YkY_{k}. When one candidate remains, rejecting reveals this candidate. In this way, every known distribution over the n!n! arrival orders arises, and for uniformly random orders, YkY_{k} can instead be uniform on n−k+1n-k+1 values. Since the distributions of the coordinates YkY_{k} are known, the algorithm can use the set consisting only of the distribution of YkY_{k} as its confidence set. The gaps at the stages that reveal YkY_{k} then vanish in the proof of Theorem 3.2, and this proof, together with that of Proposition 4.2, which applies to every arrival order, yields regret O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}) with SS summing only over the candidates. The decision tree has a node for each possible order of the candidates seen so far, but the regret bound does not depend on its size.

4.3 Optimal Stopping with Loss Aversion

Kleinberg, Kleinberg, and Oren [24] study a variant of optimal stopping with loss aversion, in which the best value seen so far serves as a reference point and accepting a worse candidate incurs a penalty. In our setting, independent candidate values X1,…,Xn∈[0,1]X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\in[0,1] with unknown distributions are observed in this order. After observing each value, the policy either accepts the current candidate and stops or observes the next one, and the last candidate must be accepted. Accepting candidate ii yields the utility xi−λ​(maxj<i⁡xj−xi)+x_{i}-\lambda(\max_{j<i}x_{j}-x_{i})_{+}, where λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 is a known loss-aversion coefficient and the maximum over the empty set is 0.

Let uiu_{i} be the node at time ii, with X1X_{1} initially observed at the root r=u1r=u_{1}. For i<ni<n, the node uiu_{i} has a stopping leaf ℓi\ell_{i} and a child ui+1u_{i+1} revealing Xi+1X_{i+1}, and un=ℓnu_{n}=\ell_{n} is the final leaf. Since utilities lie in [−λ,1][-\lambda,1], we set Γ=1+λ\Gamma=1+\lambda and define the leaf reward as

fℓi​(x1,…,xi)=xi−λ​(maxj<i⁡xj−xi)++λ1+λ.f_{\ell_{i}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i})=\frac{x_{i}-\lambda(\max_{j<i}x_{j}-x_{i})_{+}+\lambda}{1+\lambda}.

Both directions of FSD monotonicity can fail even with two candidates. Let λ>0\lambda>0 and n=2n=2. First let X1=0X_{1}=0, X2∼Bernoulli⁡(q)X_{2}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q), and q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). The optimal expected utility is qq. If only the first distribution is made larger in FSD by setting X1=aX_{1}=a, 0<a<q0<a<q, then the optimal expected utility becomes max⁡{a,q−λ​a​(1−q)}<q\max\{a,q-\lambda a(1-q)\}<q. Thus, making a distribution larger can decrease the optimal value. On the other hand, with X1=0X_{1}=0, increasing a deterministic second candidate from 1/21/2 to 1 increases the optimal value, and hence the problem is not FSD-monotone.

Proposition 4.3.

For optimal stopping with loss aversion and every λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, Assumption 3.1 holds with s1=⋯=sn=2s_{1}=\cdots=s_{n}=2, and the expected regret in the original utility is O~​((1+λ)​n​T+(1+λ)​n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{(1+\lambda)nT}+(1+\lambda)n).

Proof.

Fix arbitrary nonempty sets of distributions as in Assumption 3.1. The reward for accepting candidate ii is nondecreasing in xix_{i} and nonincreasing in every past value, since increasing a past value cannot lower the reference point. As in the proof of Proposition 4.2, the value of accepting the current candidate is nondecreasing in its value, the value of continuing is nonincreasing in it, and Assumption 3.1 holds with si=2s_{i}=2.

Let U∗U^{*} be the optimal expected utility, which lies in [0,1][0,1] since accepting the first candidate yields nonnegative utility. Proposition 3.5 with S≤2​nS\leq 2n and p=(U∗+λ)/(1+λ)p=(U^{*}+\lambda)/(1+\lambda) bounds the normalized regret by O~​(n​T​p​(1−p)+n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT\,p(1-p)}+n). Multiplying by Γ=1+λ\Gamma=1+\lambda and using (1+λ)2​p​(1−p)=(U∗+λ)​(1−U∗)(1+\lambda)^{2}p(1-p)=(U^{*}+\lambda)(1-U^{*}) yields regret O~​(n​T​(U∗+λ)​(1−U∗)+(1+λ)​n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT\,(U^{*}+\lambda)(1-U^{*})}+(1+\lambda)n) in the original utility, and (U∗+λ)​(1−U∗)≤1+λ(U^{*}+\lambda)(1-U^{*})\leq 1+\lambda proves the claim. ∎

The dependence on λ\lambda is necessary already for two candidates.

Proposition 4.4.

For every λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and T≥1T\geq 1, there are two instances of optimal stopping with loss aversion with n=2n=2 candidates such that every learning algorithm incurs expected regret at least 148​min⁡{T,(λ+2)​T}\frac{1}{48}\min\{T,\sqrt{(\lambda+2)T}\} in the original utility on one of them, even under full feedback, in which both values are revealed at the end of every round.

For n=2n=2 and T≥λ+2T\geq\lambda+2, this lower bound is at least 148​(1+λ)​T\frac{1}{48}\sqrt{(1+\lambda)T}, and hence the dependence of Proposition 4.3 on λ\lambda and TT is tight up to logarithmic factors. Appendix C proves Proposition 4.4. Appendix A.3 shows that each round runs in polynomial time when each domain is [0,1][0,1] or finite.

4.4 Stochastic Scheduling with Deadlines

In stochastic scheduling with deadlines, a single machine processes nn jobs one at a time without preemption. Job ii has a known release time ei≥0e_{i}\geq 0, a known deadline did_{i}, and a random outcome Xi∈[0,1]X_{i}\in[0,1]. The outcomes are independent across jobs and have unknown distributions. The processing time is pi​(Xi)p_{i}(X_{i}), and completing the job by its deadline earns reward ri​(Xi)r_{i}(X_{i}), where pip_{i} and rir_{i} are known nonnegative functions. We assume that pip_{i} is nondecreasing and rir_{i} has level-set complexity at most an integer si≥1s_{i}\geq 1. We can take si=1s_{i}=1 for fixed, monotone, or unimodal reward functions. Examples include rewards proportional to processing time, ri​(x)=ai​pi​(x)r_{i}(x)=a_{i}p_{i}(x), and capped rewards ri​(x)=min⁡{ai​pi​(x),bi}r_{i}(x)=\min\{a_{i}p_{i}(x),b_{i}\} with ai,bi≥0a_{i},b_{i}\geq 0. If job ii has finitely many possible processing-time–reward pairs, ordering the pairs by processing time and assigning distinct outcome labels allows us to take sis_{i} equal to half their number rounded up.

A policy starts at time 0 and repeatedly selects an unprocessed job or stops. If job ii is selected when the machine becomes free at time τ\tau, it starts at time max⁡{τ,ei}\max\{\tau,e_{i}\} and completes at time max⁡{τ,ei}+pi​(Xi)\max\{\tau,e_{i}\}+p_{i}(X_{i}). The job runs to completion even if it misses its deadline, in which case it earns no reward. Upon completion, the learner observes (pi​(Xi),ri​(Xi))(p_{i}(X_{i}),r_{i}(X_{i})) and may continue with another job. We assume that the observed pair uniquely identifies XiX_{i}, including when the deadline is missed.

Let Γ>0\Gamma>0 be a known upper bound on the total earned reward, for example, ∑isupxri​(x)\sum_{i}\sup_{x}r_{i}(x). In the tree, each node records the sequence of jobs processed so far, and their observed processing times determine the current time. The normalized leaf reward is the total earned reward divided by Γ\Gamma. Dean [11] studies stochastic scheduling with deadlines, including release times. Here, processing time and reward may depend on a common random outcome.

Correlated stochastic knapsack [19, 30], under the conditions above, is a special case with ei=0e_{i}=0 and di=Bd_{i}=B for every ii, where B>0B>0 is the capacity. Each job corresponds to an item with size pi​(Xi)p_{i}(X_{i}) and reward ri​(Xi)r_{i}(X_{i}), earned if the cumulative size including that item is at most BB. As in the standard stochastic knapsack model [10], the process stops at the first overflow, and the overflowing item earns no reward. Our analysis also covers the soft-constraint model [38], in which the overflowing item earns its reward before the process stops. If ri​(x)≤L​pi​(x)r_{i}(x)\leq Lp_{i}(x) for all ii and xx, we can take Γ=L​B\Gamma=LB under the standard convention and Γ=L​B+max⁡supxi⁡ri​(x)\Gamma=LB+\max_{i}\sup_{x}r_{i}(x) under the soft-constraint convention.

To see that FSD monotonicity can fail even under the standard knapsack convention, consider capacity B=1B=1 and two items. For item 1, take p1​(z)=r1​(z)=zp_{1}(z)=r_{1}(z)=z and let X1=xX_{1}=x deterministically, while item 2 has fixed size 1/21/2 and reward 1. For x=1/4,1/2,3/4x=1/4,1/2,3/4, the known-distribution optimal total rewards are, respectively, 5/45/4, 3/23/2, and 11. In the first two cases both items fit, while in the last case selecting only item 2 is optimal. The distribution of X1X_{1} increases in FSD, but the optimal value first increases and then decreases. Thus, the problem is not FSD-monotone.

We apply Theorem 3.7 by separating the reward of the current job from the value of the remaining jobs. The latter is nonincreasing in the current outcome because pip_{i} is nondecreasing. Their sum need not have small level-set complexity, even when the immediate reward is monotone. For example, consider knapsack with B=1B=1, item 1 with p1​(z)=r1​(z)=zp_{1}(z)=r_{1}(z)=z, and item 2 with reward 1 and size uniform on {1/m,2/m,…,1}\{1/m,2/m,\ldots,1\}. After item 1 is inserted, the optimal continuation value is proportional to x1+⌊m⁡(1−x1)⌋/mx_{1}+\lfloor m(1-x_{1})\rfloor/m, which equals 1 at x1∈{0,1/m,…,1}x_{1}\in\{0,1/m,\ldots,1\} and lies in (1−1/m,1)(1-1/m,1) elsewhere, and hence its superlevel set at level 1−1/(2​m)1-1/(2m) consists of m+1m+1 separated parts.

Proposition 4.5.

For the scheduling model above with nondecreasing processing-time functions pip_{i} and reward functions rir_{i} of level-set complexity at most sis_{i}, let S=∑isiS=\sum_{i}s_{i}. The expected regret in the original total reward is O~​(Γ​S​T)\widetilde{O}(\Gamma\sqrt{ST}).

Proof.

Fix an edge revealing job ii, its start time τi\tau_{i}, and all preceding observations. For each leaf below this edge, write fℓ=κ+χ⁡(xi)+Fℓf_{\ell}=\kappa+\chi(x_{i})+F_{\ell}, where κ\kappa and FℓF_{\ell} are the normalized rewards earned before and after job ii, and χ(z)=𝟏{τi+pi(z)≤di}ri(z)/Γ\chi(z)=\mathbf{1}\{\tau_{i}+p_{i}(z)\leq d_{i}\}r_{i}(z)/\Gamma. The reward bound ensures that χ,Fℓ∈[0,1]\chi,F_{\ell}\in[0,1]. Since pip_{i} is nondecreasing, the set {z:τi+pi​(z)≤di}\{z:\tau_{i}+p_{i}(z)\leq d_{i}\} is an initial interval of the outcome domain. At a nonnegative level, a superlevel set of χ\chi is the intersection of this set with a superlevel set of rir_{i}, and hence has at most sis_{i} interval components.

Increasing xix_{i} cannot decrease pi​(xi)p_{i}(x_{i}). Thus, no subsequent job along a fixed path completes earlier, and FℓF_{\ell} cannot increase. The sets of feasible actions remain unchanged, except that an overflow in the knapsack case allows only stopping. The immediate rewards sum to the normalized leaf reward and hence to at most 1. Theorem 3.7 and rescaling by Γ\Gamma imply the claim. For the soft-constraint knapsack model, the same proof applies with χ⁡(z)=ri​(z)/Γ\chi(z)=r_{i}(z)/\Gamma. ∎

Let OPT∗\mathrm{OPT}^{*} be the optimal expected total reward. Since the immediate rewards sum to the leaf reward, Proposition 3.8 with p=OPT∗/Γp=\mathrm{OPT}^{*}/\Gamma improves the bound to O~​(S​T​Γ​OPT∗+Γ​S)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST\,\Gamma\mathrm{OPT}^{*}}+\Gamma S). When the sis_{i} are bounded by a constant, both bounds hold with nn in place of SS, up to constant factors.

4.5 Overbooking with Group Reservations

In overbooking with group reservations, a service provider receives reservation requests from nn groups. Group ii has bi≥1b_{i}\geq 1 members, pays a fee ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0, and receives a refund ρi≥0\rho_{i}\geq 0 for each member who does not show up, where ρi​bi≤ai\rho_{i}b_{i}\leq a_{i}. The number of members of group ii who show up is Yi∈{0,…,bi}Y_{i}\in\{0,\ldots,b_{i}\}. These counts are independent across groups and have unknown distributions. We make no assumption on the dependence between the members of a group. The capacity is an integer B≥0B\geq 0, and each customer beyond the capacity incurs a cost c≥0c\geq 0. The parameters bib_{i}, aia_{i}, ρi\rho_{i}, BB, and cc are known. We take Xi=Yi/biX_{i}=Y_{i}/b_{i} as the coordinate of group ii, whose domain is {0,1/bi,2/bi,…,1}\{0,1/b_{i},2/b_{i},\ldots,1\}. The case b1=⋯=bn=1b_{1}=\cdots=b_{n}=1 is the model of individual reservations with binary show-up outcomes. Reservation management with cancellations, refunds, and no-shows is studied, for example, by Subramanian, Stidham, and Lautenbacher [35].

Before any show-up outcome is observed, the policy chooses a set UU of accepted reservations from a known family 𝒰⊆2[n]\mathcal{U}\subseteq 2^{[n]} with ∅∈𝒰\emptyset\in\mathcal{U}. At the time of service, it observes YiY_{i} for i∈Ui\in U and receives the net revenue

W⁡(U,YU)=∑i∈U(ai−ρi​(bi−Yi))−c​(∑i∈UYi−B)+.\displaystyle W(U,Y_{U})=\sum_{i\in U}\bigl(a_{i}-\rho_{i}(b_{i}-Y_{i})\bigr)-c\Bigl(\sum_{i\in U}Y_{i}-B\Bigr)_{+}.

Since the policy chooses UU before observing any outcome, this is a combinatorial semi-bandit problem. The monotonicity condition for combinatorial bandits with general reward functions [6] can fail here because of the cost of exceeding capacity.

In the tree, choosing a nonempty set UU reveals its coordinates along a chain in a fixed order, while choosing U=∅U=\emptyset leads directly to a stopping leaf. Let b¯=∑ibi\bar{b}=\sum_{i}b_{i} and C=c​(b¯−B)+C=c(\bar{b}-B)_{+}. Since −C≤W⁡(U,YU)≤∑iai-C\leq W(U,Y_{U})\leq\sum_{i}a_{i}, we take Γ=∑iai+C\Gamma=\sum_{i}a_{i}+C, assume Γ>0\Gamma>0, and normalize the leaf reward as fℓ=(W⁡(U,yU)+C)/Γf_{\ell}=(W(U,y_{U})+C)/\Gamma.

The optimal value can also be non-monotone in the show-up distribution. For example, consider a single group with b1=3b_{1}=3, a1=3a_{1}=3, and ρ1=1\rho_{1}=1, and let B=2B=2 and c=2c=2. If Y1Y_{1} is deterministic and equal to 11, 22, or 33, accepting the group yields the net revenue 11, 22, or 11, respectively, while rejecting it yields 0. Thus, the optimal value first increases and then decreases, and the problem is not FSD-monotone.

We apply Theorem 3.7 by decomposing the net revenue into the refund savings for the current group and the remaining net revenue. The former is nondecreasing in the current show-up count, while the latter is nonincreasing. Their sum, the full optimistic continuation value, can have level-set complexity that grows with the group sizes. Let b1=b2=B=a1=a2=2​mb_{1}=b_{2}=B=a_{1}=a_{2}=2m, ρ1=ρ2=1\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}=1, and c=2c=2, accept both groups, and let the set of distributions of Y2Y_{2} consist of the point masses at 0,2,…,2​m0,2,\ldots,2m. Then, the optimistic net revenue after Y1=yY_{1}=y is observed is the maximum of y+y′−2​(y+y′−2​m)+y+y^{\prime}-2(y+y^{\prime}-2m)_{+} over these values y′y^{\prime}, which equals 2​m2m for even yy and 2​m−12m-1 for odd yy. Hence, its superlevel set at level 2​m−1/22m-1/2 consists of m+1m+1 separated points, and Assumption 3.1 would require s1≥m+1s_{1}\geq m+1, which grows with the group sizes.

Proposition 4.6.

For overbooking with group reservations, the expected regret in the original net revenue is O~​(Γ​n​T)\widetilde{O}(\Gamma\sqrt{nT}), where nn is the number of groups.

Appendix C proves Proposition 4.6.

Let W∗W^{*} be the optimal expected net revenue. The total immediate reward is at most the normalized leaf reward because ai−ρi​bi≥0a_{i}-\rho_{i}b_{i}\geq 0 and the overflow cost is at most CC. Proposition 3.8 with p=(W∗+C)/Γp=(W^{*}+C)/\Gamma therefore improves the bound to O~​(n​T​Γ​(W∗+C)+Γ​n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT\,\Gamma(W^{*}+C)}+\Gamma n). Apart from Γ\Gamma, the basic bound does not depend on the group sizes bib_{i}. Appendix A.3 shows that each round runs in time polynomial in nn, tt, |𝒰||\mathcal{U}|, and b¯\bar{b}.

5 Analysis of the Upper Bound

In this section, we prove the regret upper bounds of Section 3. Section 5.1 establishes confidence-set coverage and bounds the resulting expectation errors. Section 5.2 combines these bounds with a variance budget to prove Theorem 3.2 and Propositions 3.4 and 3.5. Section 5.3 extends the analysis to immediate rewards.

5.1 Properties of Confidence Sets

To analyze adaptively collected samples, we represent the observations of each coordinate by an independent sequence of i.i.d. samples. For each coordinate ii, fix an infinite sequence Zi,1,Zi,2,…Z_{i,1},Z_{i,2},\ldots of i.i.d. random variables with distribution DiD_{i}, independently across coordinates, and interpret the jj-th revealed value of coordinate ii as Zi,jZ_{i,j}. This preserves the observation law because coordinates are independent and each revelation decision precedes observing that coordinate’s value.

The following interval bound is a consequence of the empirical Bernstein inequality of Maurer and Pontil [31, Theorem 6], and Appendix C proves it.

Lemma 5.1.

Let m≥16m\geq 16 and η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), and let P^m\widehat{P}_{m} be the empirical distribution of i.i.d. samples Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} from a distribution PP on [0,1][0,1]. With probability at least 1−η1-\eta, we have simultaneously for all I∈ℐ1I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}

|P⁡(I)−P^m​(I)|≤18​P^m​(I)​(1−P^m​(I))​βm−1+15​βm−1,where ​β=log⁡20​(2​m+1)2η.|P(I)-\widehat{P}_{m}(I)|\leq\sqrt{\frac{18\widehat{P}_{m}(I)(1-\widehat{P}_{m}(I))\,\beta}{m-1}}+\frac{15\,\beta}{m-1},\qquad\text{where }\beta=\log\frac{20(2m+1)^{2}}{\eta}. (5.1)

We now apply this bound to show that the confidence sets contain the true distributions with high probability.

Lemma 5.2.

With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have Di∈𝒞m​(D^i,m)D_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{m}(\widehat{D}_{i,m}) simultaneously for every i∈[n]i\in[n] and every 0≤m≤T0\leq m\leq T.

Proof.

For m=0m=0, the inclusion holds by definition. For 1≤m<161\leq m<16, we have bm​(z)=1b_{m}(z)=1 for every z∈[0,1]z\in[0,1] since Λ>1\Lambda>1, and hence the constraints are vacuous.

Fix ii and 16≤m≤T16\leq m\leq T, and apply (5.1) to DiD_{i} and its samples Zi,1,…,Zi,mZ_{i,1},\ldots,Z_{i,m} with η=δn⁡(T+1)\eta=\frac{\delta}{n(T+1)}. Since (2​m+1)2≤4​(T+1)2(2m+1)^{2}\leq 4(T+1)^{2}, we have β=log⁡(20​n​(T+1)​(2​m+1)2/δ)≤log⁡(80​n​(T+1)3/δ)=Λ\beta=\log(20n(T+1)(2m+1)^{2}/\delta)\leq\log(80n(T+1)^{3}/\delta)=\Lambda.

For I∈ℐ1I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, define z=D^i,m​(I)z=\widehat{D}_{i,m}(I). By (5.1), we have

|Di​(I)−D^i,m​(I)|\displaystyle|D_{i}(I)-\widehat{D}_{i,m}(I)| ≤18​z​(1−z)​βm−1+15​βm−1≤18​z​(1−z)​Λm−1+15​Λm−1\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{18z(1-z)\beta}{m-1}}+\frac{15\beta}{m-1}\leq\sqrt{\frac{18z(1-z)\Lambda}{m-1}}+\frac{15\Lambda}{m-1}
=18​mm−1​z⁡(1−z)​Λm+15​mm−1​Λm≤6​z⁡(1−z)​Λm+32​Λm.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{18m}{m-1}}\sqrt{z(1-z)\frac{\Lambda}{m}}+\frac{15m}{m-1}\frac{\Lambda}{m}\leq 6\sqrt{z(1-z)\frac{\Lambda}{m}}+32\frac{\Lambda}{m}.

The last inequality uses m/(m−1)≤2m/(m-1)\leq 2, which implies 18​m/(m−1)≤6\sqrt{18m/(m-1)}\leq 6 and 15​m/(m−1)≤30≤3215m/(m-1)\leq 30\leq 32. Since the difference is also at most 1, DiD_{i} satisfies the constraints with the radius (3.1). For each pair (i,m)(i,m) with i∈[n]i\in[n] and 16≤m≤T16\leq m\leq T, the inclusion fails with probability at most δ/[n⁡(T+1)]\delta/[n(T+1)]. A union bound over at most n⁡(T+1)n(T+1) such pairs, together with the deterministic inclusion for m<16m<16, proves that all inclusions hold simultaneously with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. ∎

The next lemma bounds the integral that arises when a function is written using its superlevel sets.

Lemma 5.3.

Let Z∈[0,1]Z\in[0,1] be a random variable, and define py=ℙ⁡(Z>y)p_{y}=\mathbb{P}(Z>y). For every η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1),

∫01py​(1−py)​𝑑y≤η+Var⁡(Z)​log⁡(1/η).\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{p_{y}(1-p_{y})}\,dy\leq\eta+\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Z)\log(1/\eta)}. (5.2)
Proof.

Let μ=𝔼⁡[Z]\mu=\mathbb{E}[Z]. We split the integral in (5.2) into the regions |y−μ|<η|y-\mu|<\eta and |y−μ|≥η|y-\mu|\geq\eta. The first part is at most η\eta, since its integration range has length at most 2​η2\eta and py​(1−py)≤1/2\sqrt{p_{y}(1-p_{y})}\leq 1/2 for all py∈[0,1]p_{y}\in[0,1]. For the second part, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality implies

∫{y∈[0,1]:|y−μ|≥η}py​(1−py)dy≤(∫01|y−μ|py(1−py)dy)1/2(∫{y∈[0,1]:|y−μ|≥η}d​y|y−μ|)1/2.\int_{\{y\in[0,1]:|y-\mu|\geq\eta\}}\sqrt{p_{y}(1-p_{y})}\,dy\leq\left(\int_{0}^{1}|y-\mu|\,p_{y}(1-p_{y})\,dy\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\{y\in[0,1]:|y-\mu|\geq\eta\}}\frac{dy}{|y-\mu|}\right)^{1/2}.

For the first integral, we use py​(1−py)≤py=ℙ⁡(Z>y)p_{y}(1-p_{y})\leq p_{y}=\mathbb{P}(Z>y) for y≥μy\geq\mu and py​(1−py)≤(1−py)=ℙ⁡(Z≤y)p_{y}(1-p_{y})\leq(1-p_{y})=\mathbb{P}(Z\leq y) for y<μy<\mu. Then, we have

∫01|y−μ|​py​(1−py)​𝑑y\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}|y-\mu|\,p_{y}(1-p_{y})\,dy ≤∫μ1(y−μ)​ℙ​(Z>y)​𝑑y+∫0μ(μ−y)​ℙ​(Z≤y)​𝑑y\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mu}^{1}(y-\mu)\mathbb{P}(Z>y)\,dy+\int_{0}^{\mu}(\mu-y)\mathbb{P}(Z\leq y)\,dy
=𝔼⁡[(Z−μ)+2]+𝔼⁡[(μ−Z)+2]2=𝔼⁡[(Z−μ)2]2=Var⁡(Z)2.\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}[(Z-\mu)_{+}^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[(\mu-Z)_{+}^{2}]}{2}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[(Z-\mu)^{2}]}{2}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{2}.

The first equality follows from the tail-integral formula 𝔼⁡[U2]=2​∫0∞t​ℙ​(U>t)​𝑑t\mathbb{E}[U^{2}]=2\int_{0}^{\infty}t\mathbb{P}(U>t)\,dt for nonnegative UU, applied to (Z−μ)+(Z-\mu)_{+} and (μ−Z)+(\mu-Z)_{+}.
