For the second integral, substitute u=|y−μ|u=|y-\mu| separately on each side of μ\mu. The integration range on either side is contained in [η,1][\eta,1], and hence

∫{y∈[0,1]:|y−μ|≥η}d​y|y−μ|≤2∫η1d​uu=2log(1/η).\int_{\{y\in[0,1]:|y-\mu|\geq\eta\}}\frac{dy}{|y-\mu|}\leq 2\int_{\eta}^{1}\frac{du}{u}=2\log(1/\eta).

The product of the two square roots is therefore at most Var⁡(Z)​log⁡(1/η)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Z)\log(1/\eta)}. Adding the contribution of at most η\eta from |y−μ|<η|y-\mu|<\eta proves the claim. ∎

The following lemma compares two distributions in the same confidence set, such as DiD_{i} and a distribution used in the optimistic update, first on unions of intervals and then on functions with small level-set complexity.

Lemma 5.4.

Let s≥1s\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0 be integers and P,Q∈𝒞m​(D^i,m)P,Q\in\mathcal{C}_{m}(\widehat{D}_{i,m}).

  1. (a)

    If m≥1m\geq 1, then for every B∈ℐsB\in\mathcal{I}_{s},

    |Q⁡(B)−P⁡(B)|≤24​P​(B)​(1−P​(B))​s​Λm+368​s​Λm.|Q(B)-P(B)|\leq 24\sqrt{P(B)(1-P(B))\frac{s\Lambda}{m}}+368\frac{s\Lambda}{m}. (5.3)
  2. (b)

    For every measurable [0,1][0,1]-valued function ϕ\phi with level-set complexity at most ss,

    |𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]−𝔼X∼P​[ϕ⁡(X)]|≤24​s​Λ​log⁡(m+1)m+1​VarX∼P​(ϕ⁡(X))+417​s​Λm+1.|\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[\phi(X)]|\leq 24\sqrt{\frac{s\Lambda\log(m+1)}{m+1}\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X))}+\frac{417s\Lambda}{m+1}.

Let m≥16m\geq 16. For (a), we first compare the empirical variance with the variance under PP on an interval I∈ℐ1I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}. Define z=D^i,m​(I)z=\widehat{D}_{i,m}(I), p=P⁡(I)p=P(I), and w=z⁡(1−z)w=\sqrt{z(1-z)}. Since z,p∈[0,1]z,p\in[0,1], we have

z⁡(1−z)−p⁡(1−p)≤|z⁡(1−z)−p⁡(1−p)|=|z−p||1−z−p|≤|z−p|.z(1-z)-p(1-p)\leq|z(1-z)-p(1-p)|=|z-p|\,|1-z-p|\leq|z-p|.

Since PP belongs to the confidence set, we obtain

w2=z⁡(1−z)≤p⁡(1−p)+|z−p|≤p⁡(1−p)+6​z⁡(1−z)​Λm+32​Λm=p⁡(1−p)+6​w​Λm+32​Λm.w^{2}=z(1-z)\leq p(1-p)+|z-p|\leq p(1-p)+6\sqrt{z(1-z)\frac{\Lambda}{m}}+32\frac{\Lambda}{m}=p(1-p)+6w\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{m}}+32\frac{\Lambda}{m}.

Completing the square yields (w−3​Λ/m)2≤p⁡(1−p)+41​Λ/m(w-3\sqrt{\Lambda/m})^{2}\leq p(1-p)+41\Lambda/m, and hence

w≤3​Λm+p⁡(1−p)+41​Λm≤p⁡(1−p)+(3+41)​Λm≤p⁡(1−p)+10​Λm,w\leq 3\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{m}}+\sqrt{p(1-p)+\frac{41\Lambda}{m}}\leq\sqrt{p(1-p)}+(3+\sqrt{41})\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{m}}\leq\sqrt{p(1-p)}+10\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{m}}, (5.4)

where the last two inequalities use x+y≤x+y\sqrt{x+y}\leq\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y} for x,y≥0x,y\geq 0 and 3+41≤103+\sqrt{41}\leq 10, respectively. By the definition of our confidence set for PP and QQ and (5.4), we now have

|Q⁡(I)−P⁡(I)|\displaystyle|Q(I)-P(I)| ≤|Q⁡(I)−D^i,m​(I)|+|P⁡(I)−D^i,m​(I)|\displaystyle\leq|Q(I)-\widehat{D}_{i,m}(I)|+|P(I)-\widehat{D}_{i,m}(I)| (5.5)
≤12​z⁡(1−z)​Λm+64​Λm≤12​p⁡(1−p)​Λm+184​Λm.\displaystyle\leq 12\sqrt{z(1-z)\frac{\Lambda}{m}}+64\frac{\Lambda}{m}\leq 12\sqrt{p(1-p)\frac{\Lambda}{m}}+184\frac{\Lambda}{m}.

We next extend (5.5) to a union B∈ℐsB\in\mathcal{I}_{s}. Write BB as a disjoint union of intervals I1,…,IkI_{1},\ldots,I_{k} with k≤sk\leq s, and define pr=P⁡(Ir)p_{r}=P(I_{r}) and p=P⁡(B)=∑r=1kprp=P(B)=\sum_{r=1}^{k}p_{r}. Applying (5.5) to each interval and using pr​(1−pr)≤prp_{r}(1-p_{r})\leq p_{r}, we obtain

|Q⁡(B)−P⁡(B)|≤∑r=1k|Q⁡(Ir)−P⁡(Ir)|≤12​Λm​∑r=1kpr+184​k​Λm≤12​s​p​Λm+184​s​Λm.|Q(B)-P(B)|\leq\sum_{r=1}^{k}|Q(I_{r})-P(I_{r})|\leq 12\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{m}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sqrt{p_{r}}+184\frac{k\Lambda}{m}\leq 12\sqrt{\frac{sp\Lambda}{m}}+184\frac{s\Lambda}{m}. (5.6)

The last inequality follows from the arithmetic-quadratic mean inequality, since ∑r=1kpr≤k​∑r=1kpr=k​p≤s​p\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sqrt{p_{r}}\leq\sqrt{k\sum_{r=1}^{k}p_{r}}=\sqrt{kp}\leq\sqrt{sp}. The complement Bc=[0,1]∖BB^{c}=[0,1]\setminus B is a disjoint union of at most s+1s+1 intervals and satisfies P⁡(Bc)=1−pP(B^{c})=1-p. Applying the same argument to BcB^{c} and using |Q⁡(Bc)−P⁡(Bc)|=|Q⁡(B)−P⁡(B)||Q(B^{c})-P(B^{c})|=|Q(B)-P(B)| yields

|Q⁡(B)−P⁡(B)|≤12​(s+1)​(1−p)​Λm+184​(s+1)​Λm.|Q(B)-P(B)|\leq 12\sqrt{\frac{(s+1)(1-p)\Lambda}{m}}+184\frac{(s+1)\Lambda}{m}. (5.7)

Since p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], we have min⁡{p,1−p}≤2​p​(1−p)\min\{p,1-p\}\leq 2p(1-p). Together with s+1≤2​ss+1\leq 2s, this shows that the smaller of the bounds in (5.6) and (5.7) is at most the right-hand side of (5.3).

For (b), define By={z∈dom⁡(ϕ):ϕ⁡(z)>y}B_{y}=\{z\in\operatorname{dom}(\phi):\phi(z)>y\} and py=P⁡(By)p_{y}=P(B_{y}). By assumption, each ByB_{y} is the intersection of dom⁡(ϕ)\operatorname{dom}(\phi) with a set in ℐs\mathcal{I}_{s}. |𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]−𝔼X∼P​[ϕ⁡(X)]|\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[\phi(X)]| =|∫01(Q⁡(By)−P⁡(By))​𝑑y|≤∫01|Q⁡(By)−P⁡(By)|​𝑑y\displaystyle=\left|\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(Q(B_{y})-P(B_{y})\bigr)\,dy\right|\leq\int_{0}^{1}|Q(B_{y})-P(B_{y})|\,dy
≤24​s​Λm​∫01py​(1−py)​𝑑y+368​s​Λm.\displaystyle\leq 24\sqrt{\frac{s\Lambda}{m}}\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{p_{y}(1-p_{y})}\,dy+\frac{368s\Lambda}{m}.

Applying Lemma 5.3 to Z=ϕ⁡(X)Z=\phi(X) for X∼PX\sim P with η=(m+1)−1/2\eta=(m+1)^{-1/2}, we obtain

∫01py​(1−py)​𝑑y≤1m+1+VarX∼P⁡(ϕ⁡(X))​log⁡(m+1)2.\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{p_{y}(1-p_{y})}\,dy\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{m+1}}+\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X))\log(m+1)}{2}}.

Substituting this estimate into the preceding bound yields

|𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]−𝔼X∼P​[ϕ⁡(X)]|\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[\phi(X)]| ≤24​s​Λ​log⁡(m+1)2​m​VarX∼P⁡(ϕ⁡(X))+24​s​Λm⁡(m+1)+368​s​Λm\displaystyle\leq 24\sqrt{\frac{s\Lambda\log(m+1)}{2m}\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X))}+\frac{24\sqrt{s\Lambda}}{\sqrt{m(m+1)}}+\frac{368s\Lambda}{m}
≤24​s​Λ​log⁡(m+1)m+1​VarX∼P​(ϕ⁡(X))+392​s​Λm\displaystyle\leq 24\sqrt{\frac{s\Lambda\log(m+1)}{m+1}\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X))}+\frac{392s\Lambda}{m}
≤24​s​Λ​log⁡(m+1)m+1​VarX∼P​(ϕ⁡(X))+417​s​Λm+1.\displaystyle\leq 24\sqrt{\frac{s\Lambda\log(m+1)}{m+1}\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X))}+\frac{417s\Lambda}{m+1}.

The second inequality uses 2​m≥m+12m\geq m+1, m⁡(m+1)≥m\sqrt{m(m+1)}\geq m, and s​Λ≤s​Λ\sqrt{s\Lambda}\leq s\Lambda. The last inequality follows from (m+1)/m≤17/16(m+1)/m\leq 17/16 and 392⋅17/16=416.5≤417392\cdot 17/16=416.5\leq 417. ∎

When PP has few support points, the following one-sided version of Lemma 5.4(b) holds for every function, which suffices for the optimistic updates.

Lemma 5.5.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0 be integers, and let P,Q∈𝒞m​(D^i,m)P,Q\in\mathcal{C}_{m}(\widehat{D}_{i,m}), where PP has at most kk support points. Then, for every measurable [0,1][0,1]-valued function ϕ\phi,

𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]−𝔼X∼P​[ϕ⁡(X)]≤24​k​Λ​log⁡(m+1)m+1​VarX∼P​(ϕ⁡(X))+417​k​Λm+1.\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[\phi(X)]\leq 24\sqrt{\frac{k\Lambda\log(m+1)}{m+1}\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X))}+\frac{417k\Lambda}{m+1}.
Proof.

Let AA be the support of PP, and let ψ(z)=(1−ϕ(z))𝟏{z∈A}\psi(z)=(1-\phi(z))\mathbf{1}\{z\in A\}. Since ψ≥0\psi\geq 0, every superlevel set of ψ\psi at a negative level is the whole domain, and every superlevel set at a level y≥0y\geq 0 is a subset of AA and hence the intersection of the domain with a union of at most kk singletons. Thus, ψ\psi has level-set complexity at most kk. Since ϕ≤1−ψ\phi\leq 1-\psi, with equality on AA, and P⁡(A)=1P(A)=1, we have

𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]−𝔼X∼P​[ϕ⁡(X)]≤𝔼X∼P​[ψ⁡(X)]−𝔼X∼Q​[ψ⁡(X)]\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[\phi(X)]\leq\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[\psi(X)]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\psi(X)]

and VarX∼P⁡(ψ⁡(X))=VarX∼P⁡(1−ϕ⁡(X))=VarX∼P⁡(ϕ⁡(X))\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\psi(X))=\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(1-\phi(X))=\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim P}(\phi(X)). Lemma 5.4(b) applied to ψ\psi with s=ks=k proves the claim. ∎

5.2 Proof of the Main Upper Bound

Before proving Theorem 3.2, we bound the expected sum of the conditional variances of a process with values in [0,1][0,1] in terms of the positive parts of its drifts.

Lemma 5.6.

Let (Yh)h=0H(Y_{h})_{h=0}^{H} be a process adapted to a filtration (ℱh)h=0H(\mathcal{F}_{h})_{h=0}^{H} and taking values in [0,1][0,1], and let dh=Yh−𝔼⁡[Yh+1∣ℱh]d_{h}=Y_{h}-\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h}] for 0≤h<H0\leq h<H. Then, we have

𝔼⁡[∑h=0H−1Var⁡(Yh+1∣ℱh)]≤𝔼⁡[YH2]−𝔼⁡[Y02]+2​𝔼​[∑h=0H−1(dh)+].\mathbb{E}\biggl[\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\operatorname{Var}(Y_{h+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h})\biggr]\leq\mathbb{E}[Y_{H}^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{0}^{2}]+2\mathbb{E}\biggl[\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}(d_{h})_{+}\biggr].

If, in addition, (Yh)(Y_{h}) is a supermartingale, that is, dh≥0d_{h}\geq 0 for every hh, then the right-hand side is at most 1.

Proof.

Since 𝔼⁡[Yh+1∣ℱh]=Yh−dh\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h}]=Y_{h}-d_{h}, we have

Var⁡(Yh+1∣ℱh)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(Y_{h+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h}) =𝔼⁡[Yh+12∣ℱh]−(Yh−dh)2=𝔼⁡[Yh+12∣ℱh]−Yh2+dh​(2​Yh−dh)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h}]-(Y_{h}-d_{h})^{2}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h}]-Y_{h}^{2}+d_{h}(2Y_{h}-d_{h})
≤𝔼⁡[Yh+12∣ℱh]−Yh2+2​(dh)+,\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h}]-Y_{h}^{2}+2(d_{h})_{+},

where the inequality follows from dh​(2​Yh−dh)≤2​dhd_{h}(2Y_{h}-d_{h})\leq 2d_{h} if dh≥0d_{h}\geq 0, since Yh≤1Y_{h}\leq 1, and from dh​(2​Yh−dh)≤0d_{h}(2Y_{h}-d_{h})\leq 0 if dh<0d_{h}<0, since Yh≥0Y_{h}\geq 0. By the tower property, 𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Yh+12∣ℱh]]=𝔼⁡[Yh+12]\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h}]]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}^{2}]. Taking expectations and summing over 0≤h<H0\leq h<H, we obtain the first claim, since the first sum telescopes:

𝔼⁡[∑h=0H−1Var⁡(Yh+1∣ℱh)]≤∑h=0H−1(𝔼⁡[Yh+12]−𝔼⁡[Yh2])+2​𝔼​[∑h=0H−1(dh)+]=𝔼⁡[YH2]−𝔼⁡[Y02]+2​𝔼​[∑h=0H−1(dh)+].\mathbb{E}\biggl[\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\operatorname{Var}(Y_{h+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{h})\biggr]\leq\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{h}^{2}]\bigr)+2\mathbb{E}\biggl[\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}(d_{h})_{+}\biggr]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{H}^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{0}^{2}]+2\mathbb{E}\biggl[\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}(d_{h})_{+}\biggr].

If dh≥0d_{h}\geq 0 for every hh, the tower property yields 𝔼⁡[(dh)+]=𝔼⁡[dh]=𝔼⁡[Yh]−𝔼⁡[Yh+1]\mathbb{E}[(d_{h})_{+}]=\mathbb{E}[d_{h}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{h}]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{h+1}], and hence the last sum is 𝔼⁡[Y0−YH]\mathbb{E}[Y_{0}-Y_{H}]. Let μ=𝔼⁡[Y0]\mu=\mathbb{E}[Y_{0}]. Since YH∈[0,1]Y_{H}\in[0,1], we have YH2≤YHY_{H}^{2}\leq Y_{H}, and 𝔼⁡[Y02]≥μ2\mathbb{E}[Y_{0}^{2}]\geq\mu^{2} by Jensen’s inequality. Hence,

𝔼⁡[YH2]−𝔼⁡[Y02]+2​𝔼​[Y0−YH]≤𝔼⁡[YH]−μ2+2​μ−2​𝔼​[YH]=1−(1−μ)2−𝔼⁡[YH]≤1.∎\mathbb{E}[Y_{H}^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{0}^{2}]+2\mathbb{E}[Y_{0}-Y_{H}]\leq\mathbb{E}[Y_{H}]-\mu^{2}+2\mu-2\mathbb{E}[Y_{H}]=1-(1-\mu)^{2}-\mathbb{E}[Y_{H}]\leq 1.\qed

We are now ready to prove Theorem 3.2.

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Let GtG_{t} be the event that Di∈𝒞i,tD_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t} for every i∈[n]i\in[n]. This event is determined by the samples collected before round tt. We call round tt good if GtG_{t} occurs. By Lemma 5.2, we have ℙ⁡(Gtc)≤δ\mathbb{P}(G_{t}^{c})\leq\delta for every tt. Since 0≤Regt≤10\leq\mathrm{Reg}_{t}\leq 1, we have

at every node. The supremum over QQ is at least the expectation under DiD_{i}, and taking the maximum over the same feasible actions preserves the inequality.

5.3 Extension to Immediate Rewards

The proof of Theorem 3.2 in Section 5.2 uses Assumption 3.1 only in the local error bound (5.12), and we prove Theorem 3.7 by replacing this bound with one that treats the immediate reward and the residual value separately.

Proof of Theorem 3.7.

6 Lower Bound

We prove Theorem 3.6 with an instance in which each coordinate ii differs from a special label with probability si/(2​S)s_{i}/(2S) and the learner must predict the signs carried by these rare values. The use of rare values is inspired by a lower-bound construction of Guo, Huang, Tang, and Zhang [17, Theorem 7] for the sample complexity of learning over product distributions. We embed the instance into a decision tree and order the labels such that the level-set complexity of coordinate ii is at most sis_{i}.

6.1 Construction

Fix integers T,s1,…,sn≥1T,s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\geq 1, let S=s1+⋯+snS=s_{1}+\cdots+s_{n}, and set

ε=14​min⁡{1,ST}.\varepsilon=\frac{1}{4}\min\left\{1,\;\sqrt{\frac{S}{T}}\right\}. (6.1)

Let J={(i,j):i∈[n],j∈[si]}J=\{(i,j):i\in[n],\ j\in[s_{i}]\}, which has SS elements. An unknown sign vector 𝜽=(θi​j)(i,j)∈J∈{−1,+1}J\boldsymbol{\theta}=(\theta_{ij})_{(i,j)\in J}\in\{-1,+1\}^{J} is fixed throughout all TT rounds.

Coordinates and distributions.

Coordinate ii takes values in a set of 2​si+12s_{i}+1 labels, which consists of a special label ⊥\bot and the pairs (j,y)∈[si]×{−1,+1}(j,y)\in[s_{i}]\times\{-1,+1\}. Its distribution is

Di𝜽​(⊥)=1−si2​S,Di𝜽​(j,y)=1+y​ε​θi​j4​S.D_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\bot)=1-\frac{s_{i}}{2S},\qquad D_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(j,y)=\frac{1+y\varepsilon\theta_{ij}}{4S}.

Equivalently, Xi=⊥X_{i}=\bot with probability 1−si/(2​S)1-s_{i}/(2S), and otherwise Xi=(j,y)X_{i}=(j,y), where the column jj is drawn uniformly from [si][s_{i}] and then the sign yy is θi​j\theta_{ij} with probability (1+ε)/2(1+\varepsilon)/2 and −θi​j-\theta_{ij} otherwise. Since ε≤1/4\varepsilon\leq 1/4, all 2​si+12s_{i}+1 labels have positive probability. Let D𝜽=∏i=1nDi𝜽D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. We identify the labels

(1,−1),⊥,(1,+1),(2,−1),(2,+1),…,(si,−1),(si,+1)(1,-1),\;\bot,\;(1,+1),\;(2,-1),\;(2,+1),\;\ldots,\;(s_{i},-1),\;(s_{i},+1)

with the points 0,1/(2​si),2/(2​si),…,10,1/(2s_{i}),2/(2s_{i}),\ldots,1 of [0,1][0,1], respectively. The label ⊥\bot thus corresponds to the point 1/(2​si)1/(2s_{i}), and only the order of the points matters for level-set complexity. Placing ⊥\bot between the two labels of column 1 keeps the level-set complexity of coordinate ii at most sis_{i}, as we verify after describing the rewards.

Decision tree and rewards.

There are no initial observations. At the root, the learner chooses a prediction vector 𝒚^=(y^i​j)(i,j)∈J∈{−1,+1}J\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}=(\widehat{y}_{ij})_{(i,j)\in J}\in\{-1,+1\}^{J}, where y^i​j\widehat{y}_{ij} predicts the sign yy when Xi=(j,y)X_{i}=(j,y). The edge chosen at the root reveals X1X_{1}, and a chain of edges then reveals X2,…,XnX_{2},\ldots,X_{n} in order, where each intermediate node has a single child and the edge revealing XnX_{n} leads to a leaf (for n=1n=1, this is the edge chosen at the root). For a realization x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), the reward f𝒚^​(x)f_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}}(x) at the leaf corresponding to 𝒚^\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}} is 1 if exactly one coordinate ii satisfies xi≠⊥x_{i}\neq\bot and this coordinate satisfies xi=(j,y^i​j)x_{i}=(j,\widehat{y}_{ij}) for some j∈[si]j\in[s_{i}], and 0 otherwise. Thus, every round reveals all coordinates regardless of the prediction, and only the distributions depend on 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}.

Level-set complexity.

We verify Assumption 3.1 with s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n}. Fix nonempty sets of distributions, a prediction vector 𝒚^\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}, a coordinate ii, and values x1,…,xi−1x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}, and let ϕ⁡(z)\phi(z) be the optimistic continuation value after Xi=zX_{i}=z is revealed. If z=(j,−y^i​j)z=(j,-\widehat{y}_{ij}) for some j∈[si]j\in[s_{i}], then coordinate ii differs from ⊥\bot and its sign is predicted incorrectly, and hence ϕ⁡(z)=0\phi(z)=0. Since ϕ≥0\phi\geq 0, every superlevel set of ϕ\phi at a negative level is the whole domain, and every superlevel set at a nonnegative level is a subset of {⊥}∪{(j,y^i​j):j∈[si]}\{\bot\}\cup\{(j,\widehat{y}_{ij}):j\in[s_{i}]\}. Such a subset consists of at most sis_{i} runs of consecutive labels, since it contains at most one label from each column and ⊥\bot is adjacent to both labels of column 1. Since a run of consecutive labels is the intersection of the domain with an interval, ϕ\phi has level-set complexity at most sis_{i}.

The next lemma shows that each incorrect sign in 𝒚^\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}} reduces the expected reward by at least a fixed amount.

Lemma 6.1.

For every 𝛉\boldsymbol{\theta} and every prediction vector 𝐲^\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}},

OPT⁡(D𝜽)−𝔼X∼D𝜽​[f𝒚^​(X)]≥ε4​S​|{(i,j)∈J:y^i​j≠θi​j}|.\mathrm{OPT}(D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}})-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}[f_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}}(X)]\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{4S}\,\bigl|\{(i,j)\in J:\widehat{y}_{ij}\neq\theta_{ij}\}\bigr|.
Proof.

Let X∼D𝜽X\sim D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, and let cic_{i} be the probability that Xk=⊥X_{k}=\bot for every k≠ik\neq i. By the union bound, ci≥1−∑k≠isk/(2​S)≥1/2c_{i}\geq 1-\sum_{k\neq i}s_{k}/(2S)\geq 1/2. For (i,j)∈J(i,j)\in J, the event that Xi=(j,y^i​j)X_{i}=(j,\widehat{y}_{ij}) and Xk=⊥X_{k}=\bot for every k≠ik\neq i has probability ci​(1+ε​y^i​j​θi​j)/(4​S)c_{i}(1+\varepsilon\widehat{y}_{ij}\theta_{ij})/(4S). These events are disjoint, and f𝒚^​(X)=1f_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}}(X)=1 exactly when one of them occurs. Hence, 𝔼⁡[f𝒚^​(X)]=∑(i,j)∈Jci​(1+ε​y^i​j​θi​j)/(4​S)\mathbb{E}[f_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}}(X)]=\sum_{(i,j)\in J}c_{i}(1+\varepsilon\widehat{y}_{ij}\theta_{ij})/(4S), and each incorrect sign decreases this value by ci​ε/(2​S)≥ε/(4​S)c_{i}\varepsilon/(2S)\geq\varepsilon/(4S) relative to 𝒚^=𝜽\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{\theta}. Since the root is the only decision and randomizing over root actions averages their values, OPT⁡(D𝜽)\mathrm{OPT}(D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) is the expected reward for 𝒚^=𝜽\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{\theta}, which proves the claim. ∎

6.2 Proof of the Lower Bound

Before proving Theorem 3.6, we show that every learning algorithm predicts each sign θi​j\theta_{ij} incorrectly with constant probability when 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} is chosen at random. For distributions P,QP,Q on a finite set 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, we write KL(P∥Q)=∑z∈𝒵P(z)log(P(z)/Q(z))\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}P(z)\log(P(z)/Q(z)) for the KL divergence and dTV​(P,Q)=maxA⊆𝒵⁡|P⁡(A)−Q⁡(A)|d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{Z}}|P(A)-Q(A)| for the total variation distance. Fix any learning algorithm, and let 𝒚^t\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{t} be its prediction vector in round t∈[T]t\in[T]. Choose 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} uniformly from {−1,+1}J\{-1,+1\}^{J} once at the beginning, and let ℙ¯\overline{\mathbb{P}} denote the probability over 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, the observations, and the internal randomness of the learning algorithm.

Lemma 6.2.

For every t∈[T]t\in[T] and (i,j)∈J(i,j)\in J, we have ℙ¯​(y^i​jt≠θi​j)≥3/8\overline{\mathbb{P}}(\widehat{y}_{ij}^{t}\neq\theta_{ij})\geq 3/8.

Proof.

Fix tt, (i,j)(i,j), and the signs θi′​j′\theta_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}} for all (i′,j′)∈J∖{(i,j)}(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})\in J\setminus\{(i,j)\}. Let 𝒵\mathcal{Z} be the finite set of possible values of the past observations Z=(Xkτ)τ<t,k∈[n]Z=(X_{k}^{\tau})_{\tau<t,k\in[n]}, and let P+,P−P_{+},P_{-} be the distributions of ZZ when θi​j=+1\theta_{ij}=+1 and θi​j=−1\theta_{ij}=-1, respectively. For one observation of coordinate ii, only the probabilities of the labels (j,−1)(j,-1) and (j,+1)(j,+1) differ, and their contributions to the KL divergence sum to ε​log⁡((1+ε)/(1−ε))/(2​S)\varepsilon\log((1+\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon))/(2S). KL(P+∥P−)=(t−1)​ε2​Slog1+ε1−ε≤3​T​ε22​S≤332,\mathrm{KL}(P_{+}\|P_{-})=\frac{(t-1)\varepsilon}{2S}\log\frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}\leq\frac{3T\varepsilon^{2}}{2S}\leq\frac{3}{32},

Let A={z∈𝒵:P+​(z)>P−​(z)}A=\{z\in\mathcal{Z}:P_{+}(z)>P_{-}(z)\}. Since aa takes values in [0,1][0,1], we have

𝔼Z∼P+​[a⁡(Z)]−𝔼Z∼P−​[a⁡(Z)]=∑z∈𝒵a⁡(z)​(P+​(z)−P−​(z))≤P+​(A)−P−​(A)≤dTV​(P+,P−).\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P_{+}}[a(Z)]-\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P_{-}}[a(Z)]=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}a(z)\bigl(P_{+}(z)-P_{-}(z)\bigr)\leq P_{+}(A)-P_{-}(A)\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{+},P_{-}).

Therefore, the error probability averaged over the two values of θi​j\theta_{ij} is

12​(𝔼Z∼P+​[1−a⁡(Z)]+𝔼Z∼P−​[a⁡(Z)])\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P_{+}}[1-a(Z)]+\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P_{-}}[a(Z)]\bigr) =12​(1−𝔼Z∼P+​[a⁡(Z)]+𝔼Z∼P−​[a⁡(Z)])\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(1-\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P_{+}}[a(Z)]+\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P_{-}}[a(Z)]\bigr)
≥12​(1−dTV​(P+,P−))≥38.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\bigl(1-d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{+},P_{-})\bigr)\geq\frac{3}{8}.

We are now ready to prove Theorem 3.6.

Proof of Theorem 3.6.

Consider the problem in Section 6.1, which satisfies Assumption 3.1 with s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n}. Conditional on 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, the past observations, and the learner’s randomness, the prediction 𝒚^t\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{t} is fixed and independent of Xt∼D𝜽X^{t}\sim D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. Hence, Regt=OPT⁡(D𝜽)−𝔼X∼D𝜽​[f𝒚^t​(X)]\mathrm{Reg}_{t}=\mathrm{OPT}(D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}})-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}[f_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{t}}(X)], which is at least ε4​S​|{(i,j)∈J:y^i​jt≠θi​j}|\frac{\varepsilon}{4S}|\{(i,j)\in J:\widehat{y}_{ij}^{t}\neq\theta_{ij}\}| by Lemma 6.1. Taking expectations, summing over tt, and averaging over 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, we obtain from Lemma 6.2

2−S​∑𝜽∈{−1,+1}JRT​(D𝜽)\displaystyle 2^{-S}\sum_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\{-1,+1\}^{J}}R_{T}(D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) ≥ε4​S​∑t=1T∑(i,j)∈Jℙ¯​(y^i​jt≠θi​j)≥ε4​S⋅T​S⋅38=332​T​ε≥164​min⁡{T,S​T},\displaystyle\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{4S}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{(i,j)\in J}\overline{\mathbb{P}}(\widehat{y}_{ij}^{t}\neq\theta_{ij})\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{4S}\cdot TS\cdot\frac{3}{8}=\frac{3}{32}T\varepsilon\geq\frac{1}{64}\min\{T,\;\sqrt{ST}\},

where the last inequality uses (6.1). Hence, RT​(D𝜽)R_{T}(D^{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) is at least this value for some 𝜽∈{−1,+1}J\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\{-1,+1\}^{J}. Since all nn coordinates are observed in every round and these observations determine the reward of every action, the lower bound holds even under full feedback. ∎

7 Conclusion

We studied SOO under semi-bandit feedback without FSD monotonicity and proposed a learning algorithm based on optimistic DP. Its regret is O~​(S​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ST}) with S=∑imin⁡{si,ki}S=\sum_{i}\min\{s_{i},k_{i}\}, where sis_{i} bounds the level-set complexity of the optimistic continuation values for coordinate ii and kik_{i} is the number of support points of DiD_{i}, neither of which the algorithm needs to know. We also showed that this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors in the worst case for all positive integers s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n} with ki=2​si+1k_{i}=2s_{i}+1, even under full feedback. With the extension in Theorem 3.7, the analysis yields regret O~​(n​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}) for all five applications in Section 4 after rescaling the rewards to [0,1][0,1], provided that, in scheduling, the reward functions have bounded level-set complexity and the observed processing time and reward identify the outcome.

Three directions remain open. First, the running time of each round is polynomial in the size of the decision tree given the suprema of the optimistic continuation values over intervals (Proposition A.3), but the tree can be exponentially large in nn, as in SBFE with general Boolean functions, and computing the suprema requires structure such as finite domains, quasi-convexity, or Lipschitz continuity (Appendix A.3). Proposition A.4 covers problems with few reachable states, and FSD-monotone problems in a known direction with finite domains reduce to exact or α\alpha-approximation algorithms for known distributions by Proposition 3.4, but it is open which other problems admit efficient learning algorithms. Second, level-set complexity is defined for real-valued coordinates, and it is open how to extend the analysis to multi-dimensional observations. Third, our algorithm builds confidence sets from the observed values, and it is open whether regret growing as T\sqrt{T} and polynomially in nn is possible without FSD monotonicity under bandit feedback, where only the reward is observed, as studied for the prophet inequality and Pandora’s box [14].

AI Methodology

We wrote earlier versions of this paper without AI assistance. These versions used the total variation of the functions ϕ⁡(z)=g¯vt​(z,xobs⁡(u))\phi(z)=\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) on intervals II for revelation edges (u,v)(u,v) as a parameter. Here, the total variation of ϕ\phi on II is the supremum of ∑j=0k−1|ϕ⁡(zj+1)−ϕ⁡(zj)|\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}|\phi(z_{j+1})-\phi(z_{j})| over all k≥0k\geq 0 and z0<⋯<zkz_{0}<\cdots<z_{k} in I∩dom⁡(ϕ)I\cap\operatorname{dom}(\phi). An analysis based on this parameter yields regret O~​(n3/4​ν​T)\widetilde{O}(n^{3/4}\sqrt{\nu T}) when the total variation is at most ν\nu. In the current version, the idea of using level-set complexity and the proof of the lower bound came from OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex and Anthropic Claude. The tools materially affected Sections 2.2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 and Appendix A. The authors verified the correctness and originality of all content, including references. We also used these tools to assist with strengthening the content and editing the language throughout the paper.

Appendix A Computational Aspects

We reduce each optimistic update to an LP, bound the running time of one round given the suprema of optimistic continuation values over intervals, and compute these suprema when the observations can be summarized by few reachable states.

A.1 Finite Reduction to Interval Masses

Fix a coordinate ii, an edge (u,v)(u,v), and observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}, and let ϕ⁡(z)=g¯vt​(z,xobs⁡(u))\phi(z)=\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}). The optimistic update h¯(u,v)t​(xobs⁡(u))=supQ∈𝒞i,t𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]\bar{h}_{(u,v)}^{\,t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)] in (3.4) maximizes over all distributions QQ on the domain of coordinate ii that satisfy the constraint in (3.2) for every interval I∈ℐ1I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, and hence, in general, over an infinite-dimensional set with infinitely many constraints. We reduce it to an LP over the masses of finitely many cells, which are formed by the sample points and the intervals between them, given the suprema of ϕ\phi on the cells. If Ni,t<16N_{i,t}<16, the confidence set consists of all distributions on that coordinate’s domain, by definition if Ni,t=0N_{i,t}=0 and since bNi,t≡1b_{N_{i,t}}\equiv 1 as in the proof of Lemma 5.2 otherwise, and the optimistic update equals supz∈dom⁡(ϕ)ϕ⁡(z)\sup_{z\in\operatorname{dom}(\phi)}\phi(z). Otherwise, write N=Ni,t≥16N=N_{i,t}\geq 16, and let D^i,N\widehat{D}_{i,N} be the empirical distribution of coordinate ii, as in Section 3.1.

Let y1<⋯<ym′y_{1}<\cdots<y_{m^{\prime}} be the distinct sample points of the empirical distribution. Partition [0,1][0,1] into the singletons {yj}\{y_{j}\}, the open intervals between them, and the two end intervals [0,y1)[0,y_{1}) and (ym′,1](y_{m^{\prime}},1], and intersect each set with dom⁡(ϕ)\operatorname{dom}(\phi). List the nonempty sets from left to right as C1,…,CMC_{1},\ldots,C_{M}, which we call cells. We have M≤2​m′+1≤2​N+1M\leq 2m^{\prime}+1\leq 2N+1. Let Nj=N⋅D^i,N​(Cj)N_{j}=N\cdot\widehat{D}_{i,N}(C_{j}) be the number of samples in CjC_{j}, and let ϕ¯j=supz∈Cjϕ⁡(z)\bar{\phi}_{j}=\sup_{z\in C_{j}}\phi(z). Each NjN_{j} is a nonnegative integer, and ∑j=1MNj=N\sum_{j=1}^{M}N_{j}=N. A cell containing a sample point is the singleton consisting of that point.

Writing qjq_{j} for the mass assigned to cell CjC_{j}, define

𝒬={q∈ℝ≥0M:∑j=1Mqj=1,|∑j=acqj−1N∑j=acNj|≤bN(1N∑j=acNj) for all 1≤a≤c≤M}.\mathcal{Q}=\biggl\{q\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{M}:\sum_{j=1}^{M}q_{j}=1,\ \biggl|\sum_{j=a}^{c}q_{j}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=a}^{c}N_{j}\biggr|\leq b_{N}\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=a}^{c}N_{j}\biggr)\text{ for all }1\leq a\leq c\leq M\biggr\}. (A.1)

We write q≤c=q1+⋯+qcq_{\leq c}=q_{1}+\cdots+q_{c} for the cumulative masses, with q≤0=0q_{\leq 0}=0.

Proposition A.1.

The set 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is nonempty and compact, and the optimistic update satisfies

supQ∈𝒞i,t𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]=max⁡∑j=1Mq∈𝒬⁡qj​ϕ¯j.\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]=\max_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}q_{j}\bar{\phi}_{j}. (A.2)
Proof.

For any Q∈𝒞i,tQ\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}, let qj=Q⁡(Cj)q_{j}=Q(C_{j}). For 1≤a≤c≤M1\leq a\leq c\leq M, there is an interval I∈ℐ1I\in\mathcal{I}_{1} with I∩dom⁡(ϕ)=Ca∪⋯∪CcI\cap\operatorname{dom}(\phi)=C_{a}\cup\cdots\cup C_{c}, and hence Q⁡(I)=∑j=acqjQ(I)=\sum_{j=a}^{c}q_{j} and D^i,N​(I)=1N​∑j=acNj\widehat{D}_{i,N}(I)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=a}^{c}N_{j}. Thus, the constraint in (3.2) for this interval II, which QQ satisfies, is the constraint in (A.1) for (a,c)(a,c), and hence q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}. In addition, 𝔼X∼Q​[ϕ⁡(X)]≤∑j=1Mqj​ϕ¯j\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\phi(X)]\leq\sum_{j=1}^{M}q_{j}\bar{\phi}_{j}. Since the empirical distribution D^i,N\widehat{D}_{i,N} belongs to 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t}, this argument shows that the vector with qj=D^i,N​(Cj)q_{j}=\widehat{D}_{i,N}(C_{j}) lies in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. As a closed subset of the simplex, 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is therefore nonempty and compact, and the linear objective ∑j=1Mqj​ϕ¯j\sum_{j=1}^{M}q_{j}\bar{\phi}_{j} with coefficients ϕ¯j∈[0,1]\bar{\phi}_{j}\in[0,1] attains its maximum on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Hence, the left-hand side of (A.2) is at most the right-hand side.

Conversely, fix q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}. Choose any point zj∈Cjz_{j}\in C_{j} from each cell, and let QqQ_{q} place mass qjq_{j} at zjz_{j}. For any I∈ℐ1I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, the set {j:zj∈I}\{j:z_{j}\in I\} consists of consecutive indices a,…,ca,\ldots,c, since the zjz_{j} are ordered. Since sample points are preserved as singleton cells, we also have D^i,N​(I)=1N​∑j=acNj\widehat{D}_{i,N}(I)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=a}^{c}N_{j}, and the constraints in (A.1) imply |Qq​(I)−D^i,N​(I)|≤bN​(D^i,N​(I))|Q_{q}(I)-\widehat{D}_{i,N}(I)|\leq b_{N}(\widehat{D}_{i,N}(I)). If no zjz_{j} lies in II, both probabilities are 0. Thus, Qq∈𝒞i,tQ_{q}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}.

Let qq be a maximizing vector on the right-hand side. For any ζ>0\zeta>0, choose a point zjz_{j} in each cell CjC_{j} such that ϕ⁡(zj)≥ϕ¯j−ζ\phi(z_{j})\geq\bar{\phi}_{j}-\zeta, which exists by the definition of supremum. Let QqQ_{q} place mass qjq_{j} at these points zjz_{j}. Since the previous paragraph applies to any choice of points in the cells, Qq∈𝒞i,tQ_{q}\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}, and hence the left-hand side is at least 𝔼X∼Qq​[ϕ⁡(X)]=∑j=1Mqj​ϕ​(zj)≥∑j=1Mqj​ϕ¯j−ζ\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q_{q}}[\phi(X)]=\sum_{j=1}^{M}q_{j}\phi(z_{j})\geq\sum_{j=1}^{M}q_{j}\bar{\phi}_{j}-\zeta. Equality follows by letting ζ↓0\zeta\downarrow 0. ∎

Section 3.2 uses the following consequence of Proposition A.1 for FSD-monotone problems.

Lemma A.2.

If the domain of coordinate ii is finite, then 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} contains a distribution that dominates all distributions in 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} and a distribution that is dominated by all distributions in 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t}, and both can be computed by solving an LP.

Proof.

If Ni,t<16N_{i,t}<16, then 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} consists of all distributions on the domain, and the point masses at the largest and the smallest points of the domain suffice. Otherwise, let the cells C1,…,CMC_{1},\ldots,C_{M} and the set 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be as above, formed in the domain of coordinate ii. Every q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} satisfies q≤M=1q_{\leq M}=1, and each constraint in (A.1) and each constraint qj≥0q_{j}\geq 0 bounds a difference q≤c−q≤a−1q_{\leq c}-q_{\leq a-1} with 1≤a≤c≤M1\leq a\leq c\leq M from above or below by a constant. Such constraints are preserved under componentwise minima of the cumulative masses, and hence, for q,q′∈𝒬q,q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Q}, the vector whose cumulative masses are min⁡{q≤c,q≤c′}\min\{q_{\leq c},q^{\prime}_{\leq c}\} also belongs to 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Since 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is compact, each q≤cq_{\leq c} attains its minimum on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and applying this closure to the minimizers for c=1,…,Mc=1,\ldots,M yields q¯∈𝒬\underline{q}\in\mathcal{Q} with q¯≤c=minq∈𝒬⁡q≤c\underline{q}_{\leq c}=\min_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}q_{\leq c} for every cc. This vector is the unique optimal solution of the LP that minimizes ∑c=1Mq≤c\sum_{c=1}^{M}q_{\leq c} over 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Let Q+Q^{+} place mass q¯j\underline{q}_{j} at the largest point of CjC_{j}, which belongs to 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} by the proof of Proposition A.1. For every Q∈𝒞i,tQ\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}, the vector (Q⁡(Cj))j(Q(C_{j}))_{j} belongs to 𝒬\mathcal{Q} by the same proof. For every x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1], the cells contained in [0,x][0,x] are C1,…,CcC_{1},\ldots,C_{c} for some cc, and hence Q+​([0,x])=q¯≤c≤∑j≤cQ⁡(Cj)≤Q⁡([0,x])Q^{+}([0,x])=\underline{q}_{\leq c}\leq\sum_{j\leq c}Q(C_{j})\leq Q([0,x]), that is, Q+Q^{+} dominates QQ. Symmetrically, the vector whose cumulative sums are all the largest, with its masses placed at the smallest points of the cells, yields a distribution in 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} that is dominated by all distributions in 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t}. ∎

A.2 Running Time with the Interval-Supremum Oracle

By Proposition A.1, each optimistic update reduces to the LP on the right-hand side of (A.2), and it remains to solve this LP and to obtain its coefficients ϕ¯j\bar{\phi}_{j}. We bound the running time of one round of Algorithm 1 on the decision tree (V,A)(V,A) under the following assumptions. First, we use the real-arithmetic model, in which arithmetic operations, comparisons, square roots, and logarithms have unit cost. Second, the algorithm can evaluate leaf rewards fℓ​(xobs⁡(ℓ))f_{\ell}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(\ell)}), test feasibility v∈𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))v\in\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), and call an interval-supremum oracle, and each of these operations has unit cost. Given an edge (u,v)(u,v) revealing a coordinate ii, observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}, and an interval I∈ℐ1I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, the interval-supremum oracle returns supz∈I∩dom⁡(ϕ)ϕ⁡(z)\sup_{z\in I\cap\operatorname{dom}(\phi)}\phi(z) for ϕ⁡(z)=g¯vt​(z,xobs⁡(u))\phi(z)=\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), or reports that I∩dom⁡(ϕ)I\cap\operatorname{dom}(\phi) is empty.

Proposition A.3.

Assume the real-arithmetic model and unit-cost access to leaf rewards, feasibility tests, and the interval-supremum oracle. Then, the policy of Algorithm 1 in round tt can be executed in time polynomial in nn, tt, |V||V|, and |A||A|.

Proof.

Since Ni,t≤t−1N_{i,t}\leq t-1 for every ii, preprocessing each sample sequence by sorting and finding distinct values and multiplicities takes time polynomial in nn and tt. Upon reaching node uu, the algorithm computes h¯(u,v)t\bar{h}_{(u,v)}^{\,t} for each feasible action vv at the current observations. For an edge with no observation, this is a leaf-reward evaluation. For a revelation edge with fewer than 16 samples, this is one oracle query with I=[0,1]I=[0,1]. Otherwise, the algorithm obtains ϕ¯j\bar{\phi}_{j} for the at most 2​Ni,t+12N_{i,t}+1 cells from the oracle and computes the optimal value of the LP of Proposition A.1. In terms of the cumulative masses q≤jq_{\leq j}, the objective and every constraint of this LP involve only differences q≤c−q≤a−1q_{\leq c}-q_{\leq a-1} with 1≤a≤c≤M1\leq a\leq c\leq M. Hence, the LP maximizes a linear function of the node potentials q≤0,…,q≤Mq_{\leq 0},\ldots,q_{\leq M} subject to upper bounds on their differences, which is the dual of an uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem with M+1M+1 nodes and O⁡(M2)O(M^{2}) arcs. By strong duality, the optimal value of the LP equals the minimum cost of this flow problem. The potentials given by the empirical distribution are feasible, and replacing the arc costs by the reduced costs with respect to them makes the costs nonnegative without changing the optimal flows. Then, the strongly polynomial algorithm of Orlin [32] computes the minimum cost with O⁡(M3​log⁡M)O(M^{3}\log M) arithmetic operations and comparisons. Since M≤2​Ni,t+1≤2​t−1M\leq 2N_{i,t}+1\leq 2t-1, the computation for each edge, including the O⁡(t2)O(t^{2}) arc costs, takes O⁡(t3​log⁡t)O(t^{3}\log t) time. The algorithm then chooses a maximizing feasible action by comparing these values.

Since the nodes visited in a round lie on a single root-to-leaf path, each of the at most |V||V| nodes is visited at most once, and at most |A||A| outgoing edges are examined in total, which proves the claim. ∎

A.3 Implementing the Interval-Supremum Oracle

The optimistic DP cannot simply be computed by backward induction, since each optimistic continuation value g¯vt\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t} is a function of the observations xobs⁡(v)x_{\mathrm{obs}(v)}, which can take exponentially or infinitely many values. The interval-supremum oracle hides this difficulty, and each query takes the supremum of the function ϕ⁡(z)=g¯vt​(z,xobs⁡(u))\phi(z)=\bar{g}_{v}^{\,t}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) of one variable over I∩dom⁡(ϕ)I\cap\operatorname{dom}(\phi). We first reduce a query to finitely many evaluations of ϕ\phi and then show how to compute these evaluations.

A query asks for the supremum of ϕ\phi over I∩dom⁡(ϕ)I\cap\operatorname{dom}(\phi), which can be an infinite set, and in the following cases, finitely many evaluations of ϕ\phi suffice. If the domain of coordinate ii is finite, a query reduces to evaluating ϕ\phi at the points of the domain in II. If the domain is [0,1][0,1], ϕ\phi is continuous, and [0,1][0,1] can be divided into finitely many known intervals on each of which ϕ\phi is monotone, a query reduces to evaluating ϕ\phi at the endpoints of the closure of II and at the division points in II. If the domain is [0,1][0,1] and ϕ\phi is continuous and quasi-convex, for example, monotone, the two endpoints of the closure of II suffice, even if the minimizer of ϕ\phi is unknown.

If the domain is [0,1][0,1] and the optimistic continuation values are LL-Lipschitz in the revealed value, a query can be approximated within η\eta by the maximum of ϕ\phi over a grid of the closure of II that contains its endpoints and has spacing at most η/L\eta/L. Each of the at most nn revelation edges below a node then adds an error of at most η\eta, and changing every coefficient of the LP of Proposition A.1 by at most the same amount changes its optimal value by at most this amount since ∑jqj=1\sum_{j}q_{j}=1. Hence, the computed values are within n​ηn\eta of the optimistic continuation values, and choosing children by them loses at most 2​n​η2n\eta in the optimistic continuation value at each of the at most n+1n+1 stages. For η=1/(4​n​(n+1)​T)\eta=1/(4n(n+1)T), these losses add at most 1/21/2 to the cumulative gap Δ\Delta in the proof of Theorem 3.2, and the regret bounds increase by at most 1, also in the refinements in which Δ\Delta enters the variance budget.

It remains to compute the evaluations. Each value of ϕ\phi is an optimistic continuation value at vv after an additional observation, and computing it requires the optimistic continuation values below vv for all further observations, whose number can grow exponentially in nn. As in a DP for known distributions, this growth disappears when the past observations matter only through a small state. For example, in stochastic knapsack (in Section 4.4) with integer sizes and an integer capacity BB, the past affects the future only through the set of inserted items and the remaining capacity, and the rewards of the inserted items are added to every subsequent leaf. With nodes representing sets of inserted items, as in the directed acyclic graph of the footnote in Section 2, the optimistic continuation value at a node is the reward collected so far plus a function of the remaining capacity, and each evaluation of ϕ\phi needs this function only at the at most B+1B+1 capacities.

Formally, a state representation consists of sets Πu\Pi_{u} for u∈Vu\in V and maps πu\pi_{u} from the observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)} to Πu\Pi_{u} with the following properties.

  1. (a)

    The state is updated by the revealed value, that is, each revelation edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) revealing a coordinate ii has a map πe\pi_{e} with πv​(z,xobs⁡(u))=πe​(πu​(xobs⁡(u)),z)\pi_{v}(z,x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})=\pi_{e}(\pi_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}),z), and each stopping edge (u,v)(u,v) satisfies πv=πu\pi_{v}=\pi_{u}.

  2. (b)

    The feasible actions depend only on the state, that is, 𝒜u​(xobs⁡(u))=𝒜~u​(πu​(xobs⁡(u)))\mathcal{A}_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})=\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{u}(\pi_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})) for some sets 𝒜~u​(π)⊆ch⁡(u)\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{u}(\pi)\subseteq\mathrm{ch}(u).

  3. (c)

    Each leaf reward is a reward of the final state plus rewards collected on the way, that is, fℓ​(xobs⁡(ℓ))f_{\ell}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(\ell)}) is βℓ​(πℓ​(xobs⁡(ℓ)))\beta_{\ell}(\pi_{\ell}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(\ell)})) plus the sum of γe​(πu​(xobs⁡(u)),xi)\gamma_{e}(\pi_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}),x_{i}) over the revelation edges e=(u,v)e=(u,v) on the path to ℓ\ell, where ii is the coordinate revealed by ee.

For knapsack, the state is the remaining capacity, or a symbol for an overflow, γe\gamma_{e} is the normalized reward of the inserted item if it fits, and βℓ=0\beta_{\ell}=0.

The optimistic DP then runs on pairs of a node and a state. Let Φℓ=βℓ\Phi_{\ell}=\beta_{\ell} at leaves, and at a non-leaf node uu, let Φu​(π)\Phi_{u}(\pi) be the maximum of Ψ(u,v)​(π)\Psi_{(u,v)}(\pi) over v∈𝒜~u​(π)v\in\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{u}(\pi), where Ψ(u,v)​(π)=Φv​(π)\Psi_{(u,v)}(\pi)=\Phi_{v}(\pi) for a stopping edge and

Ψe​(π)=supQ∈𝒞i,t𝔼X∼Q​[ψe,π​(X)],ψe,π​(z)=γe​(π,z)+Φv​(πe​(π,z)),\Psi_{e}(\pi)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\psi_{e,\pi}(X)],\qquad\psi_{e,\pi}(z)=\gamma_{e}(\pi,z)+\Phi_{v}(\pi_{e}(\pi,z)),

for a revelation edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) revealing ii. Let κu​(xobs⁡(u))\kappa_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}) be the sum of the rewards γe\gamma_{e} collected on the path to uu. Since expectations, suprema, and maxima commute with adding κu\kappa_{u}, backward induction shows that g¯ut​(xobs⁡(u))=κu​(xobs⁡(u))+Φu​(πu​(xobs⁡(u)))\bar{g}_{u}^{\,t}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})=\kappa_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})+\Phi_{u}(\pi_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})).

By Proposition A.1, each Ψe​(π)\Psi_{e}(\pi) is determined by the suprema of ψe,π\psi_{e,\pi} over the cells and over the domain. We call a finite set 𝒵e​(π)\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi) of points of the domain of coordinate ii sufficient if each of these suprema is the maximum of ψe,π\psi_{e,\pi} over the points of 𝒵e​(π)\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi) in the closure of the corresponding set. By the reductions above, the domain is sufficient if it is finite, and {0,1}\{0,1\} together with the sample points of coordinate ii is sufficient if the domain is [0,1][0,1] and ψe,π\psi_{e,\pi} is continuous and quasi-convex. Computing Ψe​(π)\Psi_{e}(\pi) then requires Φv\Phi_{v} only at the states πe​(π,z)\pi_{e}(\pi,z) with z∈𝒵e​(π)z\in\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi). Repeating this argument, the recursion evaluates Φ\Phi only at the pairs reachable from (u,π)(u,\pi), which are obtained by moving along feasible actions, keeping the state on stopping edges and applying πe​(⋅,z)\pi_{e}(\cdot,z) with zz in the sufficient sets on revelation edges. Their states are of the form πv​(xobs⁡(v))\pi_{v}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(v)}), since the sufficient sets consist of points of the domains. Let KΠK_{\Pi} be the largest number of pairs reachable from a pair (u,πu​(xobs⁡(u)))(u,\pi_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)})) over all nodes uu and observations xobs⁡(u)x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}.

For the following proposition, we work in the real-arithmetic model and assume that evaluating πr\pi_{r}, πe\pi_{e}, γe\gamma_{e}, and βℓ\beta_{\ell}, testing whether v∈𝒜~u​(π)v\in\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{u}(\pi), listing the points of 𝒵e​(π)\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi), and testing whether two states are equal all take unit time.

Proposition A.4.

Suppose that the problem has a state representation with known sufficient sets 𝒵e​(π)\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi) for every state π=πu​(xobs⁡(u))\pi=\pi_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}). Then, the policy of Algorithm 1 in round tt can be executed in time polynomial in nn, tt, |A||A|, KΠK_{\Pi}, and the sizes of the sets 𝒵e​(π)\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi).

Proof.

At each of the at most n+1n+1 visited non-leaf nodes uu with state π\pi, the policy compares the values Ψ(u,v)​(π)\Psi_{(u,v)}(\pi), which by the recursion above need Φ\Phi only at the pairs reachable from (u,π)(u,\pi). We compute Φ\Phi at each of these at most KΠK_{\Pi} pairs once, by backward induction along the edges, and we detect repeated pairs by testing states for equality. For a revelation edge ee and a state π=πu​(xobs⁡(u))\pi=\pi_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), the value Ψe​(π)\Psi_{e}(\pi) is the optimal value of the LP of Proposition A.1 for ϕ\phi minus κu​(xobs⁡(u))\kappa_{u}(x_{\mathrm{obs}(u)}), which is the optimal value of the same LP with coefficients for ψe,π\psi_{e,\pi}. These coefficients are the maxima of ψe,π\psi_{e,\pi} over the points of 𝒵e​(π)\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi) in the closures of the cells, or one maximum over the domain if Ni,t<16N_{i,t}<16, and placing these points into the cells takes time polynomial in tt and |𝒵e​(π)||\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi)|. Since each LP takes O⁡(t3​log⁡t)O(t^{3}\log t) time as in the proof of Proposition A.3, each reachable pair takes time polynomial in tt, |A||A|, and the sizes of the sets 𝒵e​(π)\mathcal{Z}_{e}(\pi). ∎

We now apply Proposition A.4 to examples. If every domain is finite, the domains are sufficient, and Proposition A.4 shows that each round runs in time polynomial in nn, tt, |A||A|, KΠK_{\Pi}, and the sizes of the domains. If every domain is [0,1][0,1] and the optimistic continuation values are LL-Lipschitz in the revealed value, the grids of spacing η/L\eta/L in the closures of the cells with η=1/(4​n​(n+1)​T)\eta=1/(4n(n+1)T) replace the sufficient sets with an error of at most η\eta in each supremum. As shown above, the regret bounds then increase by at most 1, and the proof of Proposition A.4 shows that each round runs in time polynomial in nn, TT, |A||A|, KΠK_{\Pi}, and LL, where KΠK_{\Pi} counts the pairs reachable through the grid points.

For overbooking with group reservations in Section 4.5, let the state at a node be the total number of arrivals in the groups revealed so far, which is 0 at the root and at the leaf for U=∅U=\emptyset. With γe​(π,z)=(ai−ρi​bi+ρi​bi​z)/Γ\gamma_{e}(\pi,z)=(a_{i}-\rho_{i}b_{i}+\rho_{i}b_{i}z)/\Gamma for the edge revealing group ii, πe​(π,z)=π+bi​z\pi_{e}(\pi,z)=\pi+b_{i}z, and βℓ​(π)=(C−c​(π−B)+)/Γ\beta_{\ell}(\pi)=(C-c(\pi-B)_{+})/\Gamma, the domains are sufficient, and every reachable state is an integer from 0 to b¯\bar{b}. For optimal stopping with loss aversion in Section 4.3, let ω⁡(ξ,z)=(z−λ​(ξ−z)++λ)/(1+λ)\omega(\xi,z)=(z-\lambda(\xi-z)_{+}+\lambda)/(1+\lambda) be the normalized reward for stopping at value zz when ξ\xi is the maximum of the past values. Then, Φun=ω\Phi_{u_{n}}=\omega and, for i<ni<n, Φui​(ξ,z)=max⁡{ω⁡(ξ,z),Hi+1​(max⁡{ξ,z})}\Phi_{u_{i}}(\xi,z)=\max\{\omega(\xi,z),H_{i+1}(\max\{\xi,z\})\} with Hi+1​(ξ)=supQ∈𝒞i+1,t𝔼X∼Q​[Φui+1​(ξ,X)]H_{i+1}(\xi)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{i+1,t}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\Phi_{u_{i+1}}(\xi,X)]. For a state (ξ,z0)(\xi,z_{0}), let w0=max⁡{ξ,z0}w_{0}=\max\{\xi,z_{0}\}. Appendix B Efficient Learning for SBFE with Threshold Functions

In this section, we give a polynomial-time learning algorithm for SBFE with threshold functions. Consider

F(x)=𝟏{x1+⋯+xn≥θ},θ∈[n],F(x)=\mathbf{1}\{x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n}\geq\theta\},\qquad\theta\in[n],

with positive testing costs c1,…,cnc_{1},\ldots,c_{n}, and let Γ=∑i=1nci\Gamma=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}.

At the beginning of each round tt, form the confidence sets 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} as in Section 3.1, and let

ℓi=minQ∈𝒞i,t⁡Q⁡({1}),ui=maxQ∈𝒞i,t⁡Q⁡({1}).\ell_{i}=\min_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}Q(\{1\}),\qquad u_{i}=\max_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}Q(\{1\}).

Order the coordinates by increasing ci/uic_{i}/u_{i} and, separately, by increasing ci/(1−ℓi)c_{i}/(1-\ell_{i}). We use the convention ci/0=∞c_{i}/0=\infty and break ties by index in both orders. These orders remain fixed throughout the round.

While FF is not yet determined, let mm be the number of untested coordinates and let θ′\theta^{\prime} be the number of additional 1’s needed to establish F⁡(x)=1F(x)=1. Among the untested coordinates, consider the first θ′\theta^{\prime} in the ci/uic_{i}/u_{i} order and the first m−θ′+1m-\theta^{\prime}+1 in the ci/(1−ℓi)c_{i}/(1-\ell_{i}) order. These two sets intersect because their sizes sum to m+1>mm+1>m. The algorithm tests any coordinate in their intersection and repeats until FF is determined. At the end of the round, it adds the observed values to the samples.

Proposition B.1.

For δ=1/(T+1)\delta=1/(T+1), the algorithm described above can be implemented in O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) time per round and has expected regret O~​(Γ​n​T)\widetilde{O}(\Gamma\sqrt{nT}) in the original testing cost.

Proof.

The endpoints ℓi\ell_{i} and uiu_{i} for all coordinates can be computed in O⁡(n)O(n) time from the sample counts using (3.1) and (3.2). Sorting the two orders once per round and scanning them at each of the at most nn steps takes O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) time.

We next bound the regret. Write the normalized reward from Section 4.1 as f=f0+f1f=f_{0}+f_{1}, where fb(σ,x)=f(σ,x)𝟏{F(x)=b}f_{b}(\sigma,x)=f(\sigma,x)\mathbf{1}\{F(x)=b\} for b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. For q∈[0,1]nq\in[0,1]^{n}, write Bernoulli⁡(q)=∏iBernoulli⁡(qi)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)=\prod_{i}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_{i}), and define

Vb​(q)=maxσ⁡𝔼X∼Bernoulli⁡(q)​[fb​(σ,X)].V_{b}(q)=\max_{\sigma}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)}[f_{b}(\sigma,X)].

Then OPT⁡(Bernoulli⁡(q))≤V0​(q)+V1​(q)\mathrm{OPT}(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q))\leq V_{0}(q)+V_{1}(q). The increasing orders of ci/qic_{i}/q_{i} and ci/(1−qi)c_{i}/(1-q_{i}) attain V1​(q)V_{1}(q) and V0​(q)V_{0}(q), respectively [4, 33]. This also holds when some probabilities are 0 or 1 by continuity, since there are finitely many policies.

Fix a round tt, and write ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓn)\ell=(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{n}) and u=(u1,…,un)u=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}). Consider a stage with mm untested coordinates and remaining threshold θ′\theta^{\prime}. On every completion with F⁡(x)=1F(x)=1, a fixed order of the remaining coordinates tests all of its first θ′\theta^{\prime} coordinates. Moving any one of these coordinates to the front therefore does not change the testing cost on such completions. The same holds for completions with F⁡(x)=0F(x)=0 and the first m−θ′+1m-\theta^{\prime}+1 coordinates. By induction on mm, the policy σt\sigma^{t} of the algorithm has the same testing cost as the ci/uic_{i}/u_{i} order on inputs with F⁡(x)=1F(x)=1 and as the ci/(1−ℓi)c_{i}/(1-\ell_{i}) order on inputs with F⁡(x)=0F(x)=0. Hence, it attains V1​(u)V_{1}(u) under Bernoulli⁡(u)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(u) and V0​(ℓ)V_{0}(\ell) under Bernoulli⁡(ℓ)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\ell).

For a fixed testing order, f1f_{1} is nondecreasing and f0f_{0} is nonincreasing in each xix_{i}. Thus, V1V_{1} is nondecreasing and V0V_{0} is nonincreasing in each qiq_{i}. Let pi=ℙ⁡(Xi=1)p_{i}=\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=1) and p=(p1,…,pn)p=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}). If every DiD_{i} belongs to 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t}, then ℓi≤pi≤ui\ell_{i}\leq p_{i}\leq u_{i} for every ii, so V1​(u)≥V1​(p)V_{1}(u)\geq V_{1}(p) and V0​(ℓ)≥V0​(p)V_{0}(\ell)\geq V_{0}(p). Proposition 3.4(b) with α=1\alpha=1 and K=2​nK=2n therefore applies to f1f_{1} with Qt=Bernoulli⁡(u)Q^{t}=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(u) and to f0f_{0} with Qt=Bernoulli⁡(ℓ)Q^{t}=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\ell). Adding the two bounds yields

∑t=1T(V0​(p)+V1​(p)−𝔼⁡[f⁡(σt,Xt)])=O~​(n​T).\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(V_{0}(p)+V_{1}(p)-\mathbb{E}[f(\sigma^{t},X^{t})]\bigr)=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nT}).

This bounds the normalized regret since OPT⁡(Bernoulli⁡(p))≤V0​(p)+V1​(p)\mathrm{OPT}(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p))\leq V_{0}(p)+V_{1}(p). Multiplying by Γ\Gamma gives the regret bound in the original testing cost. ∎

Appendix C Omitted Proofs

Proof of Proposition 4.4.

Let n=2n=2, let X1=1/2X_{1}=1/2 with probability 1, and let X2∈{0,1}X_{2}\in\{0,1\} with ℙ⁡(X2=0)=q\mathbb{P}(X_{2}=0)=q. Stopping at the first candidate yields utility 1/21/2, and continuing yields expected utility (1−q)−q​λ/2=1−(λ+2)​q/2(1-q)-q\lambda/2=1-(\lambda+2)q/2. Let q0=1/(λ+2)q_{0}=1/(\lambda+2), ε=18​min⁡{q0,q0/T}\varepsilon=\frac{1}{8}\min\{q_{0},\sqrt{q_{0}/T}\}, and q±=q0±εq_{\pm}=q_{0}\pm\varepsilon. Continuing is optimal for q=q−q=q_{-}, and stopping is optimal for q=q+q=q_{+}. In both instances, the other action loses (λ+2)​ε/2=116​min⁡{1,(λ+2)/T}(\lambda+2)\varepsilon/2=\frac{1}{16}\min\{1,\sqrt{(\lambda+2)/T}\} in expected utility.

Under full feedback, X2X_{2} is revealed at the end of every round regardless of the action, which provides more information than semi-bandit feedback. Fix a round tt, and let P+P_{+} and P−P_{-} be the distributions of the t−1t-1 previous samples of X2X_{2} for q=q+q=q_{+} and q=q−q=q_{-}, respectively. The action in round tt depends only on these samples and the internal randomness of the learning algorithm. The KL divergence between the distributions of one sample is at most their chi-squared divergence (q+−q−)2/(q−​(1−q−))(q_{+}-q_{-})^{2}/(q_{-}(1-q_{-})). Since q−≥7​q0/8q_{-}\geq 7q_{0}/8 and 1−q−≥1/21-q_{-}\geq 1/2, we have

KL(P+∥P−)≤(t−1)​(2​ε)2q−​(1−q−)≤64​T​ε27​q0≤17.\mathrm{KL}(P_{+}\|P_{-})\leq\frac{(t-1)(2\varepsilon)^{2}}{q_{-}(1-q_{-})}\leq\frac{64T\varepsilon^{2}}{7q_{0}}\leq\frac{1}{7}.

By Pinsker’s inequality, dTV​(P+,P−)≤1/14<1/3d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{+},P_{-})\leq 1/\sqrt{14}<1/3. As in the proof of Lemma 6.2, the probability of the wrong action in round tt, averaged over the two instances, is at least (1−dTV​(P+,P−))/2≥1/3(1-d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{+},P_{-}))/2\geq 1/3. Summing over the rounds, the average of the regrets on the two instances is at least T3⋅116​min​{1,(λ+2)/T}=148​min​{T,(λ+2)​T}\frac{T}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{16}\min\{1,\sqrt{(\lambda+2)/T}\}=\frac{1}{48}\min\{T,\sqrt{(\lambda+2)T}\}, and hence the regret on one of them is at least this value. ∎

Proof of Proposition 4.6.

We verify the conditions of Theorem 3.7 with si=1s_{i}=1, for which S=nS=n. Consider the edge revealing group ii in the chain for an accepted set UU. Let ϱ\varrho be the sum of aj−ρj​(bj−Yj)a_{j}-\rho_{j}(b_{j}-Y_{j}) over the groups jj of UU revealed before group ii, and let JJ be the set of groups of UU revealed after group ii. The only leaf below this edge is the leaf for UU, and with Yi=bi​xiY_{i}=b_{i}x_{i}, its reward is κ+χ⁡(xi)+F\kappa+\chi(x_{i})+F, where κ=(ϱ+ai−ρi​bi)/Γ\kappa=(\varrho+a_{i}-\rho_{i}b_{i})/\Gamma, χ⁡(z)=ρi​bi​z/Γ\chi(z)=\rho_{i}b_{i}z/\Gamma, and

F=1Γ​(∑j∈J(aj−ρj​(bj−Yj))−c​(∑j∈UYj−B)++C).F=\frac{1}{\Gamma}\Bigl(\sum_{j\in J}\bigl(a_{j}-\rho_{j}(b_{j}-Y_{j})\bigr)-c\Bigl(\sum_{j\in U}Y_{j}-B\Bigr)_{+}+C\Bigr).

The function χ\chi has level-set complexity at most 1 because it is nondecreasing. Moreover, χ,F∈[0,1]\chi,F\in[0,1] by ρj​bj≤aj\rho_{j}b_{j}\leq a_{j} and ∑j∈UYj≤b¯\sum_{j\in U}Y_{j}\leq\bar{b}. The residual reward FF is nonincreasing in xix_{i}, and the sets of feasible actions do not depend on xix_{i}. Finally, the immediate rewards sum to ∑j∈Uρj​Yj/Γ≤1\sum_{j\in U}\rho_{j}Y_{j}/\Gamma\leq 1. Theorem 3.7 and rescaling by Γ\Gamma imply the claim. ∎

Proof of Lemma 5.1.

We apply Maurer and Pontil’s theorem [31, Theorem 6] to the function class {𝟏I:I∈ℐ1}∪{1−𝟏I:I∈ℐ1}\{\mathbf{1}_{I}:I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\}\cup\{1-\mathbf{1}_{I}:I\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\}. Its uniform covering number at scale 1/m1/m on 2​m2m points is bounded by the number of distinct value patterns. On ordered points x1≤⋯≤x2​mx_{1}\leq\cdots\leq x_{2m}, an interval selects a consecutive block, yielding at most (2​m+1)2(2m+1)^{2} patterns. Including the complementary indicators yields at most 2​(2​m+1)22(2m+1)^{2} patterns, which combines with the factor 10 in their theorem to produce the numerator in β\beta. The sample variance of either indicator is m​P^m​(I)​(1−P^m​(I))/(m−1)m\widehat{P}_{m}(I)(1-\widehat{P}_{m}(I))/(m-1), yielding the variance term in (5.1). ∎
